utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Court is back in session. Please be seated. Registrar, will you have the accused brought in, please? Before proceeding, let us make sure everyone can hear me. Can you hear me, Mr. Erdemovic? Mr. Babic? Mr. Erdemovic, is that working? Is that all settled? Can you hear me, sir? Mr. Erdemovic, you can hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No translation, there is no translation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can the Office of the Prosecutor hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. So the Court is back in session. Before hearing the Defence, which will be calling its witnesses, the Tribunal believes that it has not been fully informed as regards a certain number of points. These relate, in particular, to any mitigating or aggravating circumstances relative to the accused and, as things now stand, the Tribunal cannot fulfil its mission which is to hand down an appropriate sentence. So, under these circumstances, the Judges of this Trial Chamber believe it is necessary to put some additional questions to Mr. Drazen Erdemovic under oath. So, would you kindly step up to the table? Would you take the solemn oath and answer the questions we will be putting to you? MR. DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC, recalled. Examined by the Court, continued.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Please take the solemn declaration, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. In your testimony yesterday, Mr. Erdemovic, you said that you had served in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you had served in the Croatian army of Bosnia- Herzegovina and you had served in the Serb Army. The point is that before joining the HVO, the Croatian army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you were in the Bosnia-Herzegovina army. Can you please give us some further information about this, that is to say, more specifically, when did you join the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? When did you leave that army and why did you leave it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact date when I joined the army. I joined that army when I received call up papers from the military department in Tuzla. I went to the Local Commune building, to the Territorial Defence building at that time, and I was first there and then later on I was with the Mortar Unit. The army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I left it somewhere in 1992, in November, I believe. I left the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina because, as I told you yesterday, I wanted to avoid any possible participation in combat operations because I did not care about fighting. I just wanted to have some lighter tasks and I carried out tasks that were normally carried out by the military police. I was securing the headquarters and some checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, you joined the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina exactly when, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I received call up papers by the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What month, what year, not necessarily the date, what month, what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sometime in the end of May when the conflict between the former JNA and members of the MUP in Tuzla broke out, at the end of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Erdemovic, you said that you were not a member of the army of the Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but that you were obliged to serve therein. Does that mean that military service was obligatory there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosnian Serbs, yes, of course, there was an obligation to serve; only those who had enough money and who were able to buy up their lives and avoid the military obligation, they were free, and those people were well off. They had private cafes, petrol stations, small companies and all kinds of property. I had no means to pay, so I had to join the army. I simply did not have any means to feed my family; I had to. Nobody asked me whether I wanted to join the army. If I did not do it of my own will, they would have taken me. They would have beaten me, and they used to do it, they used to beat you. They used to give you a uniform and simply take you to the front and the punishment was to stay one month at one of the worst front lines. That is how it was. Everybody knows that, not only me, everybody here, all the detainees here know how it happened. I did not want that war, but nobody asked me, "Drazen Erdemovic, did you vote for the SDS, HDZ, SDA?" No, nobody. I voted for the reform forces in Tuzla who won only in Tuzla. Tuzla was not in favour of a war option, but nobody asked me whom I voted for, because I was against the war and I proved it by voting for that party. I was not - I did not want a war. I had no motives. I had no motivation to go to war. Is there anyone here who can understand me? My wife is a Serb. It is not her fault that she is a Serb and I am a Croat, and it is not her fault that Serbs and Croats were waging war. Was I supposed to hate her because she is a Serbian or to hate a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Drazen Erdemovic, please listen to me just for a second. Listen to me closely. I want you to be sure - I am now speaking. I am the Presiding Judge here, sir, just to be perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are putting these questions to you because you are before a Tribunal, that is to say, an impartial and independent body. Why are we putting these questions to you? It is because we need this information to judge you in the most impartial and independent way possible. Please let that be clear to you. Then you will understand what the point is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, but let me explain this to you. I do understand this, but this is the twelfth time that I am repeating my story, the story of how my life has been destroyed. Please try to understand me. This is the twelfth time I am doing this. When I testified during Rule 61 hearing against Mladic and Karadzic, when I went back to my cell, I just could not get up for three days. I got an ulcer. It was diagnosed by doctors. It was so detrimental for my health. Then I had to undergo this operation here in Holland and everything became stable again, but then yesterday again you saw me, you saw how I testified. I do apologise for my behaviour when I took off my shirt when I showed my injuries. I appeal to your understanding, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Drazen Erdemovic, it is precisely because we are trying to understand, but we do not only want to understand Mr. Drazen Erdemovic, we want also to understand the people that died. That is what we are trying to understand because we have to hand down a decision. We want it to be fair and impartial, taking account of you and taking account of the victims. So I shall pursue these questions, even if it is the twelfth time you have to answer them. I am sorry for that but, from what you said yesterday, there are some things that are lacking. I cannot help that, nor can my colleagues here if both in what was put forward by the Prosecution and the Defence we find that there are still some lacunas. So I am sorry if it is the twelfth time, but for us, Judges, it is the second time. I am sorry if prior to that you talked to journalists and you had other people you had to talk to, but we are now going to put seven or eight further questions to you, because in this kind of setting when you talk about mitigating or aggravating circumstances, you need something to substantiate them. This is why I suggest we deal with this very calmly. Please make this effort for the International Criminal Tribunal. That is your assurance. It is an assurance for you that we are providing you with. Now, with regard to mitigating circumstances and, in particular, with regard to the duress that you have mentioned - you have touched on that point several times - the Tribunal is wondering what your level of information was, because it is not quite clear to us how in this territory of Republika Srpska with all these events going on that you were not more informed as to what was going on through the media etc.. Yesterday you did not fully answer that question, so let me reword it for you more clearly. Please try calmly and serenely to answer this question for the Judges, not for the Prosecution, not for the Defence but for the Judges, because at the end of day it is the Judges who are going to decide as to your fate. So, please, sir, remain calm and try to respond to these questions. When you went to Republika Srpska, what kind of information did you have as to the policies being pursued by the political and military leaders there? As a soldier, did you have access to any information, in particular as regards the policies and the practices of the Serbian Army and, in particular, the notion of a greater Serbia and the issue of ethnic cleansing? So please make an effort. This is very important to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will give you an answer right away. Your Honours, I will try to speak, to tell you, to explain to you the best I can. I was not involved in politics, but I will do my best. Of course I used to watch TV. I listened to the news. To be frank, ethnic cleansing was not publicly discussed that much. I do not believe that any TV of any country would do that, that they would show their own government, their own army who is in charge of the country, that they show them ethnically cleansing a particular territory. Whether they really planned to do so, whether that was their objective, I do not know. I had a very low rank. I had a very low, unimportant position. I could not know anything about their plans, but I used to watch TV, for example, at the moment a conflict between Croats and Muslims broke out and then I asked myself, why, why such a conflict between Muslims and Croats because they were together at the beginning of the war, fighting against the Serbs? I kept asking myself, but I did not know the answer and I still do not know the answer, but probably Croatian and Muslim authorities do know the answer. Then I used to watch Fikret Abdic, for example, and his Muslims fighting against other Muslims, Muslims from Bihac, the Fifth Corps of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Why? I do not know why. That is what I used to watch on the TV of Republika Srpska. They just showed at that time when I was there, they just showed the conflict between Croats and Muslims and Croats between Muslims and Muslims. Muslims calling Fikret Abdic to help them fighting Serbs - fighting Muslims from the Fifth Corps of Bosnia and Herzegovina in their fight against the Serbs. So I kept asking myself, why are they fighting each other if the war is between Croats and Serbs, Muslims and Serbs? I kept asking myself, how come all of a sudden there is a conflict between Muslims and Croats? I do not know the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your division and your Unit there, when these events at Srebrenica were happening, were there any racist comments? Were fellow soldiers saying, "We are going to kill them all. We are going to exterminate them. We are going to wipe them out"? It is the general feeling we want to have. You have told us -

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What more, what better example than the one that I just told you about, that the events that happened, and even the Prosecution admitted that they were not aware of that, of that crime which took place at that spot I told you about? What more can I say? A thousand people perished there and I heard that in Nova Kasaba many people were killed, Nova Kasaba and elsewhere. What else can I tell you? It is a crime. First of all, I would like to say that I chose Mr. Babic. It is true that some Serbs have destroyed my life but not all of them and I will try to explain this to you. I chose Mr. Babic for my counsel because I had told my story to a journalist and I was arrested in Yugoslavia, and the media in Yugoslavia said that I was a Croatian spy and that I was crazy. I chose Mr. Babic because he is an honest man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, I would like to put another question. Go right ahead. Yes, I suppose you have had recourse to Mr. Babic because you think he is the best counsel for you, but that is not within our camp, but you have not fully answered my question. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will. I wish to explain. I told you the media in the Republika Srpska started manipulating my case and manipulating me as an individual. They publicly said that I was a Croatian spy. So that is how the media in the Republika Srpska started spreading stories about my being a Croatian spy. I do not know whether you understand what I just wanted to explain to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put another question to you, just to see what kind of knowledge you had about the general environment. There are some things that are not clear to us with regards to how you were spending your time. You said yesterday, for instance, that on the morning of 14th July when you were, if I have this right, at Vlasenica, you had received a new order. There was a task, a mission, that was to be carried out and you were told that you were to go to Zvornik. Is that right? That is what you said yesterday? That is right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I did not say it was on 14th. I said it was on 16th when I came back from the funeral of my colleague from Trebinje. So I came back in the evening of 15th, me and the colleagues who went with me to the funeral. So in the morning of 16th I got up and Gojkovic, Brano, who at the time was the Commander of the Unit, he told us to get into a vehicle to carry out an assignment and I learned at that time that he was going to headquarters in Zvornik and that is what I said yesterday. If I did not explain it properly, thank you. I thank you for asking this question again because I would like everything to be perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, you said it was 16th, but we have had a look at this. We have cross-checked. We have looked at the transcript of your statements at the hearing against Messrs. Karadzic and Mladic. That is something else we have taken into account. We are looking at what you said yesterday, but we are also looking at what you have said in the past. That is true, you have made 12 statements. It is a good thing we only have two of them because it a matter of us looking at the consistency, in particular, when it comes to the information provided by the Prosecution. As regards 14th to 16th, it was not clear to us how you were spending that time. So what happened on 14th and 15th? There is no point on dwelling on 16th, but on 14th and 15th. So there was a soldier, a friend of yours, who was buried?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will tell you right away, the interpretation I received, you said there was a discrepancy, there is a hole, between the 14th and 16th, a void. Yes, in the morning of 13th - in the evening of 12th, we came to Vlasenica from Srebrenica to the base and I learned that our Commander had overturned, had had a traffic accident, in an APC and a soldier, a colleague of ours, was killed in that accident and who was in that APC. So on in the morning of 13th I was assigned to go to the funeral together with several other colleagues, to Trebinje. So we stayed, we spent one day travelling to Trebinje and there were some war operations going on, so you had to take a longer route from Vlasenica to Trebinje. We spent the whole day travelling. We arrived in Trebinje in the morning around 4 o'clock. So on 14th we buried our comrade and we came back on 15th. Do you now understand those dates?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. With regard to duress which you have invoked, you said that you were opposed to the orders from your superior. So maybe you could give us some information. Our fellow Judges and myself have a few questions on this score. You said that there was this Lieutenant Colonel who was giving you orders. You did not, however, identify him. You know that well. At the same time you said that you were under the orders of Gojkovic, Brano. My question is, can you give us some further information as to the identity of the superiors who were there where the execution was taking place? You had some reluctance as regards executions. Who did you address yourself to? This is the key question. You said, "I was under physical and moral duress". You were under orders and you had to obey them. That is what your defence is built around. Who was there? Who were your superiors? What are their names and who did you express your reluctance to co-operate to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall begin with who the Commander of our Unit was, the Unit I was a member of, a former Unit. The Commander was Lieutenant Milorad Pelemis. He used to be Lieutenant First Class but then he was promoted and became Lieutenant, Lieutenant Milorad Pelemis. On 16th July, the Unit in which I was, the Unit which carried out the executions of Muslims from Srebrenica, that Unit was commanded on that day by Brano Gojkovic. He was from the Vlasenica platoon. When you ask me whom I said that I did not wish to participate in the killings. I said that openly in front of Brano and other soldiers, but nobody gave me his support. I do not know why, but nobody did at that time. Later, when this Lieutenant Colonel arrived, I mentioned him yesterday, when he came back - sorry, when I said that I did not wish to take part in that, Brano Gojkovic very clearly told me, "If you do not wish to do it, stand in the line with the rest of them and give others your rifle so that they can shoot you". That is how it happened. I said that I would say the truth and that is how it happened. You can believe it or not, but I know what the truth is and I know what hurts me and what has destroyed my life. Later on when Lieutenant Colonel arrived, Brano did not say anything, but the Lieutenant Colonel said that there were 500 Muslims in the culture hall who were about to escape and that we should go there. I said loud and clear to the Lieutenant Colonel that I do not wish to participate in this any longer and that I was nobody's robot for killing, and if he had told me that I had to, I would have shot him. It was at that occasion that I received support of several of my colleagues, but that is how it was. I knew I would have problems because of that. I knew that there would be a report against me and that is what happened later on. I was shot by a man who had bragged about having killed the majority of Muslims that day, and that is Savanovic, Stanko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that clear answer. The next question. This has to do with the wounds which you showed the Tribunal yesterday. Could you explain more in detail the circumstances of that incident? Could you tell us who shot you? "It was because of my reaction to the Colonel". This is part of your defence. So please go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I indicated yesterday, Kremenovic was with another group who had refused an assignment and I did not know that. We were in Vlasenica at that time, and Pelemis together with Salapura went there trying to convince them to carry out the assignment, but they refused to do it. They did not want to take part in this dirty business, because Kremenovic knew Salapura very well and he knew about dirty business he was involved in. So, Kremenovic came back with his Unit on 22nd July 1995 and we also arrived in Bijeljina from Vlasenica, and I met with Kremenovic at that time. I told you yesterday that I was drinking heavily in those days after Srebrenica and that I did not spend much time with my family at home. So Kremenovic told me what had happened. I did not tell him everything about what had happened, but he told me, "They are not going to take me - they are not going to use me for their dirty business", and I just started crying because I was thinking to myself, "I have been abused". So we were discussing that and Kremenovic told me that on 23rd at 12 o'clock there was supposed be a meeting and that we would request to separate from the Vlasenica platoon from those people who were nationalist, that we would request a replacement of Pelemis and so on. I do not know. All kinds of things could have happened before that meeting. But on that night, myself, Kremenovic and another colleague were shot by Stanko Savanovic. I will tell you now so that you know -

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stanko, are you sure that it was Stanko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will explain. When we got out of the cafe it was already midnight. It was closing time, and I was quite drunk. I wanted to go home, but Kremenovic told me, "Come with me, let's have a chat. God knows what will happen tomorrow. Let's see what we can do tomorrow" because the trusted me. He saved my life two times. He saved me when I was injured. It was upon his intervention that I was transferred to the hospital in Belgrade and later on he saved me once again before I went into contact with that journalist. I did not want to make any trouble for that man who is now living in the federative Republic of Yugoslavia. So, Stanko Savanovic fired at me and another member of our Unit and at Kremenovic also. This other member of our Unit was a Muslim. I am a Croat. Kremenovic is a Serb. He is a Lieutenant and he is Deputy Commander of our Unit. I will tell you how come I know that it was ordered by Salapura and Miso. I can show this to you if I - I could show this to you if I had a newspaper. Each incident that takes place in a cafe or in the street is prosecuted by military tribunal in Bijeljina, but investigating Judges established that Stanko Savanovic, without any cause, without any reason whatsoever, had attempted a triple murder. He had attempted to kill three persons. I again asked for an explanation. Well, OK, I am a Croat, there is nothing I can do about it, Ustasha, he would not be held responsible for me. He would not be held responsible for this Muslim either. When I asked him, "Are you going to bring a charge against him?" He told me, "Well, what for? I can talk but nobody will listen to me". A simple soldier shooting at an officer trying to kill him, attempting a murder, and not be held responsible for that - and you know why, because he was protected by Colonel Salapura who is the Chief Intelligence Officer of the main headquarters of the army of Republika Srpska. That is my explanation. He was under his orders and that is what Kremenovic confirmed to the journalist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were wounded. Did you take any legal action? Were there any proceedings? Did the military police take down a report or what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was in a very serious condition. My wife was told to get ready for the worst because they did not believe that I would survive. I had two serious injuries to the stomach and one injury to my lungs. I had two operations at the same time in Bijeljina. It was all at Kremenovic's intervention. The operation at Bijeljina did not succeed. So, thanks to Kremenovic and some other colleagues from my Unit, I was transferred to Belgrade and I am grateful for doctors from the Belgrade hospital because I survived. After the operation I was in a very difficult state again. I could not talk and so on. Investigators from Bijeljina arrived then, and they asked me whether I wanted to testify as a witness and whether I wanted to say whether Stanko Savanovic really wanted to kill us. Of course that was his defence. He said that he was not going to kill, it was not his intention to kill anyone. Well, I could accept an explanation of a friend or a colleague. I could accept the explanation of a stray bullet; but three bullets, one Muslim as a victim, Kremenovic and myself, I simply cannot understand. Nobody can explain that to me. So I said, "I do not wish to bring charges" because I can tell about the result right away. How was I supposed to confront them? I knew that it would be to no avail. That is what they told me, some authorities, when they visited me in the hospital in Belgrade. So I was called to the Court to testify, but nobody was there. They just enquired, they interviewed this owner of the cafe and he said that Savanovic simply took out his pistol and started shooting at his colleagues, colleagues from his Unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You had said that your military contract was going to expire in 1997. Under what circumstances did you stop being a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was wounded and I was not receiving my salary regularly. I really do not know when was the last time I received a salary. A year and a half has passed after I was wounded. I have not received any salary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Coming back to the facts themselves, the last question which the Tribunal would like to ask you. This is a technical problem, unfortunately, but we would like to have your opinion about this. You had a kalashnikov. This is a kind of a machine gun which shoots bursts of fire. You also stated during the Karadzic hearing or yesterday that you had also shot individual shots. I had asked you whether you had seen your victims. We do not know whether it was bursts or fire or whether you were aiming specifically at the civilians there, aiming at their backs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will tell you. I said I shot single shots. I was not aiming. When I was pulling the trigger, I would close my eyes and I would turn around so as not to see those people falling down. That is how it happened. I am telling you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Tribunal has a last question, but one not to Mr. Erdemovic, I would like to ask Mr. Babic. Mr. Babic, yesterday you spoke about a decision of the Supreme Court of the Yugoslav Republic. Do you not hear?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, not the Supreme Court of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, but the competent court of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have the decision?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Could we ask the Registrar to have it translated for the Trial Chamber Judges? Would you please give it to the Registrar? (Handed) Thank you. Mr. Erdemovic, yesterday you said that you wished to speak about a certain number of mitigating circumstances. The Tribunal will now ask you to go back right now, take your place where you were sitting before, unless my colleagues have other questions they would like to ask. You can take your ordinary place here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, and I am sorry about my outburst yesterday when I showed my wounds. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will now go back to the agenda of our hearing, as we set it yesterday. We had planned that we would hear Mr. Babic who wanted to bring in witnesses to speak about the mitigating circumstances, because that is the line of defence which was chosen. Mr. Babic, would you first like to make a preliminary report? How do you plan to organise the presentation of your witnesses? I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wish to say the following. Yesterday and today I think that many mitigating circumstances became more obvious and clearer. In order to have a complete picture, I had proposed at our last status conference that we receive a report, an expert report, of psychiatrists and that this be part of the case, the first and the second report; also to obtain a report on the current state of health and the general state of health of the accused Erdemovic. I am sure that the Registry has already done this. On the other hand, there are other mitigating circumstances. What is the character of Erdemovic? Therefore, I deemed it necessary to have the witnesses established by the Court heard. I will make a final statement at the end, but first I would like to hear the witnesses. So, perhaps we can hear a witness first that Erdemovic, when it was in his power, when he decided of his own freewill that he saved his 21 life. That will be the first witness and then we will hear the second witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Since these witnesses are covered by protective measures, for our work, are you speaking about witness X or Y that you would like to hear first?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is all the same to me. I propose that we start with X, but it can also be Y first. It is all the same to me.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Prosecutor has no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No objection at all.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then I suppose we could begin with X then. Registrar, would you please recall the measures which the Chamber took in order to assure the protection of witness X? Perhaps you could also state which have been taken for Y. Would you please recall what measures have been taken by the Trial Chamber for X and for Y?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Further to two recommendations of the Legal Department of the Registry and the Witness and Victims Unit, the Trial Chamber has set up protective measures which include not naming the persons by their names - they will be known as X and Y - and to protect their entrance into the courtroom which will, with the leave of the Trial Chamber, mean that the curtains will be lowered and that we will not show the faces on the television screens. The faces will be hidden and the voices will be distorted. Should it be necessary, the Trial Chamber could say that the transmission of the images will be delayed by 30 minutes which would allow us, if necessary, to correct any inaccuracies or any problems. So perhaps we need five minutes now in order to set up the courtroom before witness X can come in.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will suspend the hearing. (10.55 a.m.) (The Court adjourned for a short time) (11.10 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Would you please sit down? Turning to the Registrar, have the provisions that are necessary been made that needed to be made so that we can now bring in witness X? Before we do bring him in, I would like to say to the Prosecution - do you hear me, sir - that the decision of the higher court which was given to us by Mr. Babic and which was given to the Registrar is being translated, according to what Mr. Marro has just said to me, and will, of course, be given to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Turning to the Registrar? WITNESS X, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Witness X, do you hear me in your language? Do you hear me? THE WITNESS [In translation]: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You will first take the oath. I would like this oath to be given to witness X. Read the oath, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall say the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be seated, please? Witness X, the Tribunal thanks you for coming at the request of Mr. Babic from the Defence. Please realise that you are in the confines of an International Tribunal. You are before Judges. All the measures of protection which you have asked for have been taken. Therefore, you can speak without fear and with the greatest serenity possible. Nonetheless, the Tribunal must be sure of your identity but since your identity cannot be revealed to the public, the Tribunal would like you to write your name on a piece of paper, your first name, including your date and place of birth, as well as your profession and your nationality.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your name, your first name.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The date of your birth, the place of your birth, your nationality and your current profession. Do not fear. This will be brought to the attention of Mr. Babic. He will be shown the document. Then it will be shown to the Tribunal. I am going to show it to my colleagues. This document will be placed under seal in the case files of the Tribunal and never transmitted. Mr. Babic, I give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Examined by MR. BABIC

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: I shall put my questions very directly and I shall also ask the witness to give very direct answers. My first question: Does the witness know the accused Drazen Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when have you known him? If you could tell me on which occasion did he meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No translation].

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the witness. The interpreters cannot hear the witness at all.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We do not hear the witness which means that the interpretation booth does not hear the witness. We can begin again, please. Perhaps the microphone has to be turned up. Do the interpreters hear now? Would you please answer, witness X?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, the microphone does not work, says the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do the interpreters hear witness X?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No. The English booth does not hear him.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, perhaps you could ask your question again and this way we can be sure that the interpreters have understood what the witness X is saying so that everybody can hear the answer properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: The first question was, does the witness know the accused Drazen Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: The second question, when did they meet and on what occasion? Does he remember correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In November 1992. We were in the same Unit in the 115th Brigade of HVO military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were together then in the HVO, can you tell the Court something about Drazen as a person, what was he like as a person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not in that Unit together for a long time but he was like other people. He did not really distinguish himself in relation to others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when was Drazen in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Drazen was in the HVO, I do not know the exact dates, I do not know the exact dates, about three months. Then because, because he transferred people of Serb nationality across the line, he was transferred to another Unit and then he was not on the same Unit with me any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know after that where Drazen was and what he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was transferred to another Unit on the line. I did not meet him after that, until August 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until August 1994. Where was that in August 1994? Where were you then and could you say in what capacity Drazen was there? Could you tell us everything about this meeting that took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day I went to the battalion command to take weapons to go to the line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Belonging to what army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was on Mount Majevica, it was not far away, and I saw Drazen and another soldier with him. They were by themselves. They stopped me. This army had a scorpio weapon and he wanted to shoot me and Drazen jumped up and said, "No, let the man go. Don't shoot him". Then another one came up from my back. Then I told Drazen, because I knew him, I did not know these other two men, "What are you doing there?" I saw him wearing a Serb Army uniform, and I said, "What are you doing there in that uniform?" and these people started explaining something in a very impudent manner, and he said, "(redacted), don't ask me too much, too many questions. I have to do this. I tried to run away to Switzerland. They would not let me", and that was it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: I kindly request the witness not to mention names, X.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We remind witness X that if he has to be protected, the people whom he is speaking about should also be not named. There is a delay. We have a system which permits us to transmit things with delay which allows to correct any mistakes which may have been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: On that occasion were you, frankly speaking, fearful for your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I was. I did not have anything and they had weapons on them. This other man had a weapon too and I did not know what he would do. Of course it was only natural, it was only human, to be afraid in a situation like that. I was, frankly speaking, truly afraid that they would shoot me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They detained me there for about two or three hours. I asked hem to let me go, but these two would not but then it was strictly at Drazen's insistence that they let me go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then he gave me a box of cigarettes, a pack of cigarettes, and he also gave me some pistol ammunition. He said, "Take care, comrade, be careful".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this your last meeting with Drazen Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that Drazen Erdemovic saved your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at any rate he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Prosecutor, have you any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No, thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Judge Odio Benito? Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I will call you Mr. X, sorry. I shall not say your name. You mentioned that you knew Mr. Erdemovic during your service in the military police, that is right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Which is the Serbian Croat police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was strictly HVO military police.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, the Bosnian Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The Bosnian Croat, and he was dismissed from this police because he helped the Serbs to go out from Croatia to Serbia or to the Bosnian-Serb region, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not from Croatia, from part of the federation that was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He helped people of Serb nationality to go not to Serbia but to Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: To Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he help any others? Did he help Muslims to go back to Bosnia or did he help Croats to go back to the Croatian region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if he could have helped Muslims then or Croats to go here and there because he was on territory that was held by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Muslims were not going from the territory of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the Serb entity.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you alone when he tried to save you or did you have other people with you which he also tried to save?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was alone that day.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you think there is any special reason why he would have chosen to save you; in particular, the relationship, what kind of a relationship exactly did you have with him? Was it just because you belonged to the same country, let us say? A. I do not know his reasons, but probably we were in the same Unit. He had known me for three or four months while we were together. JUDGE RIAD: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Tribunal thanks you, witness X. You will now be taken out of the courtroom the same way that you were brought in. The Registrar will be responsible. For the time being do not move. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Since the curtains are drawn, we can now bring in Witness Y using the same procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Yes. WITNESS Y, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Witness Y, first of all, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Please read the oath that you will take before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare to say the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Witness Y, at the request of the Defence, you have agreed to testify before this Tribunal. You are in front of Judges and we have taken all precautionary measures for protecting you that you asked for. For that reason you may speak with full serenity and no fear to Judges who will listen to you answering the questions which Mr. Babic will ask you, Mr. Babic who is the counsel for Drazen Erdemovic. As we did for the previous witness and so that we can ensure what your identity is, we will ask you to write your name, your first name, the date and place of birth, nationality and profession on the piece of paper which has been given to you. Witness Y, the information which you have just given to the Tribunal and to the Defence and to the Prosecution will be put under seal and never revealed. So this will ensure that your testimony is made in full serenity, as I said before. I give the floor immediately to Mr. Babic now who will ask the questions that he considers to be the most appropriate. Examined by MR. BABIC

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Yes, rightly so, Mr. Chairman, the most appropriate questions in this role of witness. May I start with the same question again? Does the witness know Drazen Erdemovic? Since when has the witness known Drazen Erdemovic and how does the witness know Drazen Erdemovic as a person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Drazen Erdemovic. I met him in January/February 1993. We were friends. That is all.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: This friendship, was this just a friendship between the two of you or with several other people of the same age, your classmates from school or from the neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This friendship was not between the two of us only. It was a multinational friendship with all acquaintances of ours, regardless of nationality, from school, our friends that we went out together with.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Does that mean that, in your company, among your friends, there were Muslims, Croats and Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In this company of friends, did anybody ever ask questions as to religion, nationality, etc?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know Drazen's views and did Drazen ever present his views on these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know that Drazen was not a nationalist at all. It was not important to him who was what nationality. It was only important for him that we knew how to be friends and that we had a sense of humour.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Does that mean that in your company of friends nobody ever raised that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody. That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Is it the same now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did Drazen like this company of friends?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did his friends like him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What was his character like? Was he a vivacious person, good natured or did he like to pick a fight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not like to pick a fight. He was a vivacious person. He was always outgoing.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know Drazen well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know anything about where Drazen went during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know that Drazen was mobilized and went into the Croat army, the Muslim army? Do you know when he left the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina under the control of the Muslim army and the Croatian army, when and where did he go to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know Drazen when he was in the army of Bosnia- Herzegovina, but I know him when he was in the HVO. I know that he left it on 3rd November and then he went over to Republika Srpska. He spent two months there without joining any army and then he had to join the Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How did he join the Serb Army? Was he mobilized?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, everybody had to go to the army regardless of who and what he was, so he had to. He tried to avoid it. He tried to find a way out. He tried to get out but it was not possible. He had to join the army.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did Drazen ever tell you something about the war, what his attitude towards the war was and what his attitude towards the army and these armies in general was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Drazen did not enjoy the war at all, and I am certain that he hated the war and that he hated the army, but he simply had to do all of it.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know what the consequences were for a person who did not respond to mobilization by any army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were fateful, if you know what that means, fateful consequences, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I am going to address a question to you belonging to the present. In the environment in which you live today, in the narrower or broader sense of the word, are people commenting on the trial of the accused Drazen Erdemovic? Could you say how people are commenting on this? Did you comment on this in the company of your friends or what kind of company did you comment upon this? Was this a multinational company of people and what do people think about this and how do they assess Drazen's role before this Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is only natural that people are commenting upon his trial. However, regardless of the nationality they belong to, everybody says that Drazen was not that kind of person and that Drazen had to do this under pressure, that he would not kill of his own freewill but only if he was forced to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Is this being commented upon by Croats, Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, mostly by people who are in the environment in which I live, who are important people there, who hold important posts.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Are these people Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You said that Drazen was against the war, against the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he try to do something in order not to go into the war or not to join the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At first he tried to find a way out of the federation to get out to Republika Srpska. However, this was only in passing so that he would go abroad, but the situation was such that nobody managed to get out, especially if he was a male. Everybody had to go to the army and the consequences were fateful, disastrous.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you know about the fact that the accused Erdemovic was wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Is it known in the environment in which you live that this happened and why this was done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody comments on this in the same way. He was wounded only so that he would be eliminated so that he would not testify about the acts, the terrible things, that took place there.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: These comments, do they continue until the present day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you read newspapers? Do you watch television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The mass media, do they comment on this trial and in what way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. It depends. If we watch Serb television then Drazen is a traitor, and if we watch Muslim television then Drazen is a witness who will corroborate war crimes of higher people in the Serb Republic, so it differs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. Prosecution, have you any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No, no questions, your Honour. Examined by the Court

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Excuse me for calling you (redacted) Y". I will call you (redacted) Y". You said that you met Mr. Erdemovic in January 1993. Where was that exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a disco club.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Yes, was it in Republika Srpska or was it not there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was in the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was in the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Then he went after that to Republika Srpska. What forced him to go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. Republika Srpska was just supposed to be in passing. He was supposed to go abroad, to a better life abroad.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: He stayed from November '93 to April '94 in Republika Srpska without any job or any work, is that right, and then he joined, after he joined the Bosnian Serb Army. What did he do during this period before joining the Bosnian Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was moving from one place to another then. When things would become critical in one place, then he would move to another place, just to dodge the army.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You said that when you met him he had friends from every, let us say, nationality - Croatian, Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did his feelings change during the war gradually towards some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did he remain friends with the Muslims or were there some quarrels off and on during the period of fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Drazen remained a friend. We have an example. In Republika Srpska, we had two friends who were girls, Muslims, and now they are in Tuzla. I am still friends with them. Now, when I was leaving they told me to give their best to Drazen.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The Defence asked you about the echo of his being here on trial. You mentioned that the Serbs consider him as a traitor. Why do they consider him as a traitor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because he agreed to tell the world about the crimes over there, and that in the long run it was the small fry who were held responsible and that those who were responsible for issuing commands are not being exposed.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: From the Muslim side, is it not mentioned, no mention of his participation in the executions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is being mentioned, but all of them say that Drazen was only an executor of orders and that the main culprits should be found and those who issued these orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Witness Y, throughout these journeys which took the accused from one camp to another, did your relationship with him remain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Were you always in a relationship with him? Did you ever give him any advice? Were you afraid for him? Did you give him any advice? Would he call you, for example, sometimes, let you know what was going on with him? Would you say something to him? What did you say to him about all this moving about that he was doing, this dangerous moving about? What were you doing? If I am not being indiscreet, what kind of advice were you able to give him or did you give him? Would you say, "Things are all right" or "You cannot do anything else" or did you say, "Be careful" or "I do not agree"? Did you have the freedom to express your opinion and, if it is possible, could you tell us what that opinion was?

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: For example, when he was wounded, these serious wounds that he received, you knew about them? What did you know about the circumstances surrounding the wounds that he received? Did you see him then in the hospital? Were you able to find something out? What could you tell the Tribunal about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only found out that these were his comrades at arms from Republika Srpska and that one of them had wounded him, but this was all according to the orders of his Commander because they had suspected Drazen, because of the case from 1994, I think. There was a suspicion concerning Drazen as far back as then.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Going back to you, Witness Y, to your opinion, because after all you are here to express your feelings, once again, what image do you have of this journey across the war through the area controlled by Croats, then to Republika Srpska, then dozens of Muslims are killed? What is your feeling about it, your own feeling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that Drazen is not the kind of person who would enjoy killing. I think that he was ordered to do that and that he had to do that, and he had to do it because of his family which was then in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When one receives an order, do you believe that these orders must always be obeyed? What do you feel about that, you personally, you, Witness Y?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the situation in Republika Srpska, that orders have to be obeyed and carried out otherwise the consequences are fateful for the family and, in this particular case, the accused, Drazen Erdemovic too.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Throughout this period did he keep you informed about his moods, about his opinions? Could you say something to us about that or about common friends that you had? Did he tell you, "This is a dreadful war" or, on the contrary, did he say, "I just cannot do anything else" or that "You have to be too brave to do something else. I have no way of being other than I am"? Could you tell us what his mood was, his mental state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (No translation). He was fed up and that he wanted to get out, not to participate in the war at all in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: The accused told us that at one point he began to drink. Did he drink before that? What could you answer about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Drazen, I mean, before we would all drink depending on our mood and if we were celebrating something we would all have a drink, and when he would return from his assignments Drazen starting consuming more alcohol and he withdrew. He did not want to talk about anything. He was nervous. He sought comfort in alcohol.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Since the beginning of this trial, even before that, ever since the accused has been here in The Hague, have you received any threats? Do you receive any threats? Do you feel that you are in danger?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. There were some conflicts but nothing terrible.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness Y. I have the feeling that Mr. Babic perhaps wished to ask another question? No. I believe that Judge Riad does have another question he would like to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (redacted), you mentioned (and we have all evidence) that Mr. Erdemovic joined the Bosnian Serb Army in April 1994 after having spent five months almost in Republika Srpska without doing anything. That is right, from November 1993, I think, to April 1994 he was in Republika Srpska and you said going from one place to another to avoid trouble, and -

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: - in 1994 he was forced to join the Bosnian Serb Army. Would it not have been possible for him during these six months before to go back to the Croatian part where he belonged and to avoid joining the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You do not know. In that time were you in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Was it known what their execution squads, or what they called the Sabotage Units and so on, were doing? Was the idea of ethnic cleansing in the information media or was it completely put aside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The media did not speak of this at all. I know the case of Srebrenica. The Serbs were saying that the Muslims had moved out and that Srebrenica was empty and that the Serbs simply walked into an empty town. Nobody had any idea of the killings and of the torture of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You also mentioned that it was inevitable to obey the orders and to execute the orders given to kill. It so happened that Mr. Erdemovic was brave enough, apparently from the evidence, that he refused the action once under Pelemis and he was degraded. But he could refuse; and then another time he refused to go to the hall, the school, and kill the 500 Muslim prisoners there. He could do that. Then it was possible, in your opinion, to avoid executing the killings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only way to avoid this killing was for him to stand in line with them, for him to be a victim too as well as his family, which was then in Bijeljina. That was the only way.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So the family would have been in danger, according to the system in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you have another question you wish to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Related to the question put by distinguished Judge Riad. Let us set the record straight. These six months that he spent there after leaving Muslim and Croat controlled territory, he did not spend these six months only in Republika Srpska. He spent these six months on the territory of Yugoslavia too, in Serbia, going from one place to another trying to find a way out. Then when mobilizations began in Serbia and Yugoslavia, fearful of being detained or maybe some other measures were taken then, I do not know, but he says that he was afraid. Then he went back to Bijeljina and then he was mobilized in Bijeljina and then he had no choice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this precision. Would any response be forthcoming from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Witness Y, the Tribunal thanks you for having come this far to testify at the request of the accused. You will be taken out in the same way that you were brought in so that you may go home under the best conditions possible. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The Registrar has informed me that there will be three changes - I can speak openly now - the references which through the questions which all of us have asked will have allowed the witness to be identified. How much time do we need? Would you like to recall them or, rather, recall what these changes are?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It seemed to me that under 11.45.24 and 11.24.00, 11.58.02 and 12.00 should be removed completely. 11.45.24, 11.46.24 and 11.58.02.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The Tribunal agrees. Is that all? My colleagues as well as myself would like to inform the parties of the following decision. We have now heard the witnesses. We have heard what has to be said about mitigating circumstances which, as I have said before, is the line of defence adopted by the Defence. The accused Erdemovic yesterday stated that he wished to speak about the mitigating circumstances under oath, of course. I will ask him if he wishes, and if his counsel agrees, to come back under oath to speak about these mitigating circumstances. If he does agree - I see that Mr. Babic is nodding yes; therefore he can come back - after that we will suspend the hearing and resume at 2.30 when we will hear the final statement of the Prosecution and the Defence by Mr. Babic. Then the final statement not under oath made by Drazen Erdemovic will put an end to this hearing. Mr. Babic, I understand that you agree with this way of working and so does the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is now five minutes after 12.00. Drazen Erdemovic, would you please come to the stand to speak about the mitigating circumstances? MR. DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC, recalled.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can you hear me? It is not a matter of going back over the facts of the case. We have gone into them in quite some detail. We have gone into it a bit too frequently, but yesterday morning I cut you off, as it were. So we would like to hear you speak your mind and to put forward evidence in connection with mitigating circumstances. Now, there are several elements involved here. There are superior orders, there are threats, there is duress, be it moral or physical in nature. You said that you wanted to address these issues. You are under oath, so if there are questions you do not want to answer you need not do so, but that goes - or, rather, it is the opposite. You have to answer the questions put to you by the Prosecution, by the Defence and by the Judges. THE ACCUSED: Honourable Judges -

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did you hear what I said?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, I heard you, I am sorry. First of all, I would like to tell you that while I was a child, when I went to school, the elementary school, and later on I went to secondary school, I have never ever been a nationalist. I have never ever hated anyone. That is the way how I was brought up and educated at school by my parents. The environment in which I lived was a multinational environment where Serbs, Muslims and Croats lived together. So I was not a nationalist. I cannot say, I cannot tell you, I do not know why things happened the way they did in the former Yugoslavia. This country was known to the world as a country in which many people lived together, people who got along well with each other. Nobody hated anyone. People used to visit each other, visit them for family reunions. When we would go to do our military service in the JNA, it was a special occasion for everybody in Bosnia. It meant that you were able, you were healthy enough, to do your military service in the former JNA. That is how it was in Bosnia. I do not know about the rest of the country. It did not really matter whether you were a Serb or a Croat. That is how it was in the area where I lived, as far as I know. After the death of, I can now say, the person I respected and loved (and I still regret that), after the death of comrade Tito, several years after that, everything went the wrong way in Yugoslavia. You could tell it from the fact that this conflict, this war, broke out. The first conflict broke out in Slovenia between the JNA and the Slovenian Territorial Defence, and then the conflict moved down to the territory of Republic of Croatia in 1990/91. Later in '92, as you know, it broke out in the area where I lived, in my Republic, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So, I am speaking frankly. I know I am under oath. I served my military service in December 1990. I joined the JNA. I went to do my military service because I believed in the former Yugoslavia. I used to love that country and that army. I thought that they were honest, but later I realised that things had changed. So I went to do my military service and did it in Belgrade. I was with the military police and in 1991 I was sent -

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just one second, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Later I was transferred to Slavonia - believe that is the name of the area - in the vicinity of Vukovar, to be precise. I was a member of the military police. I was securing a checkpoint. I will explain to you what kind of assignments we had. We were in charge of checking vehicles that were passing by, relevant papers, weapons, because there was a war there. So we had to check who issued the permission for carrying weapons and things like that. Then at that time certain paramilitary units appeared. They were causing lots of problems in Belgrade. That is why we, the JNA, were in charge of controlling that. They called us a communist army and traitors. So I did my military service in an honest way, the way I believed in, and I was not a nationalist. I was never a nationalist. I had Slovenian colleagues in the JNA, Serbs, Hungarians, and I do not know who else, you name it, Albanians. You know how many different nationalities live in Yugoslavia. We never ever discussed politics and background of other soldiers. We were only discussing those paramilitary units because those people caused us problems, and how they had been established, I do not know. I was just a regular soldier. Even the officers did not know. We were even fired at by them once when we tried to stop them. Thank God I returned home safe and sound from my military service but, unfortunately, I did not spend much time with my parents and the conflict soon broke out in BH and then in Tuzla on 15th May 1992. Then I was called to the army - and I forgot to tell you last time; when I came back from Belgrade I received call up papers from the barracks in Tuzla which was controlled by the JNA. I received that paper, and I went there together with - I took the paper and I told them, "Well, gentlemen, I do not want to go to any army. I do not want to take part in any war. I have seen a war. I do not know what it is. I have done my military service. I have done my year", so I just throw away that paper and I left. But nobody came to arrest me because at that time problems started between the JNA and the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina - at least that is what they were showing on TV in BH. So after that, as I told you, general mobilization started. So I received again call up papers. I reported, and I reported to the Territorial Unit in my area, the area of the Donja Dragunja Local Commune. There were Serbs there, Croats, Muslims. There was a kind of defence from so-called aggression against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is what they told us. They told us that they were setting up units. After that the war started in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You no longer simply defended yourself, your home and your town, but we were sent outside Tuzla, for example, to the Brcko area. Those were the assignment, they deployed units there. But I knew what the war was all about. I had seen it back in '91 when I was with the JNA. I had seen many things that other people had not seen. I saw people getting killed. I was at that checkpoint and I could see wounded soldiers being transported, hundreds of them. Some of my colleagues were burnt alive in their tanks and I was telling those stories when I returned home. I was in favour. I was supportive of the reformist party in the area of Tuzla. They said that they were in favour of peace, that they did not want war. Unfortunately, the war happened in Tuzla and in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well. So, as I said, I was in with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but after that, wishing to avoid the war, because I had lost four of my very best friends, people with whom I had spent more time than with my own brother, one of them was a Muslim, one of them was a Croat, one Serb and one Albanian who lived in Bosnia, four very good friends of mine. So I joined the HVO, and I will tell you this. I was a member of the military police and we received orders to arrest people, to put uniforms on them and to send them to the front line. I rebelled at that time at the command. I told them that I did not want to arrest anyone. I did not want to be responsible for the death of anyone. I did not want to be exposed to criticism of mothers whose sons were killed and so on. I did not want to be responsible for that. So, one other incident; there was an offensive in the area of Brcko, and some of my colleagues and some other people whom I did not know were killed in Brcko, five of them. This is what hurts most and this will hurt me for the rest of my life. The Commander of this HVO Unit, HVO Brigade, came to see our Commander who was in charge of the military police, and he said that he needed four men to go to the exchange with the Serbian side so that they can get back the bodies. So we got all the necessary information, names, surnames, dates of birth and so on. They gave us four names, four dates of birth of those people and also the unit they - the units they belonged to. But when we got to Brcko I did not get in there because there were just too many bodies there and the exchange took place in Brcko, I cannot remember exactly where - maybe later. Then this friend of mine from the military police told me, "Drazen, could you please come and see whether this is the person? Let us not make a mistake", because those people did not have any kind of identification papers with them. They were naked. They did not have anything. So I went there. I recognised the man. I found the fifth person as well, the fifth HVO member who had been killed. So the Commander of the HVO had forgotten one of his men, one of his men who was killed in Brcko. This shows you just how much he cared for his people. He told me four persons and I found a fifth one. Now, I think you can understand what made me flee that war, what kind of injustice I had been through and everything that had happened. So, as I told you, I did not go to the Republika Srpska because in order to join their army and stay there. It was just supposed to be a stop over on my way to Switzerland because I did not want to take part in that war; I did not want to. I simply could not bear seeing my former neighbours committing such crimes. I simply could not understand how such things could happen. I could not understand. Maybe somebody else could, but I could not. So, as I already told you, in the Republika Srpska I was first in Bijeljina and then I went for Janja. Then some soldiers from a paramilitary unit tried to arrest me in Janja. They wanted to kill me. They knew I was a Croat. They wanted me to report in their unit and all kinds of things happened. So I fled to Serbia together with my wife. We just kept moving about Serbia from one place to another, and then this general mobilization of Bosnians took place in Serbia. They wanted all Bosnians in Serbia to go back to the Republika Srpska. That was a government's order. So I was afraid, I was afraid of everything, and I did not know what to do. I kept thinking it would have been easy if I had been alone, but I did not know what to do with my wife who was pregnant at that time. It would have been easy for me to flee across the border, even without papers, but I knew that if I got caught they would kill me because I was a Croat and I did not have any identification papers, except for my ID from Tuzla. I did not have any passport. So I went back to Republika Srpska and I went to a cousin of my wife. We went to Foca. When we got to Foca - I told you about that yesterday - when we got there, I had to register myself somewhere. I had some kind of paper from Republika Srpska and, being a Croat, it was difficult. This man told me, "Drazen, OK, you have been with the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You admitted that. You have been with the HVO. You did not commit any crimes. You helped Serbs. Just don't stay in Foca. It is not safe for you, you, a Croat". That is all he had to tell me, because they could not guarantee that I would survive there. The wife could stay, that is what they told me, but I could not. That was his advice. So I took his advice and I went back to Bijeljina. As I told you, I was stopped by the civilian police in Bijeljina. They requested some kind of permission which I did not have, but this Serb who was with me at the time confirmed that I was the person I was. He told them everything about me. He knew certain details about me. So they told me that I should immediately report to the town hall and that I should be given a green card, a green refugee card, with all details of my whereabouts, and people I was living with and so on. I think that that green card should have been obtained from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, if you have that document from that country. However, nothing, no accommodation, no papers were possible, it was possible to obtain them because I was not a member of any army. So I had to join the army. Why? To survive. So this man who was working in the military department who was in charge of deploying, assigning, people to various units, asked me about my name, "Drazen Erdemovic, who are you? What are you?" and I did not hide it. I told him I was a Croat. So he kept staring at me, "How did you get out? Who let you out?" Then I started my story from the beginning; how I helped Serbs in Tuzla, how I am not a criminal. But I had to be a member of an army so I went to all kinds of details to make my story believable. So after that he told me that there was this Unit and there is one Muslim in this Unit, one Slovenian, one Croat, and there is another unit which is a paramilitary Unit, and some people from that unit wanted to kill me after I left Tuzla and if I had not fled to Serbia they would have probably killed me at that time.
