So I joined this first Unit and the first thing that I asked was when I saw those two people, two Croats, "What is the task of this Unit? What are they in charge of? Is there any dirty business that they are supposed do?" They told me, "Drazen, the Commander is a very good man and he has never ever issued any order to liquidate anyone". That is what they told me. I talked to this Commander and he had talked with those Croats whom he trusted more. He wanted to know more about myself and so on, because I told my story to the authorities of the Ministry of the Interior, how I arrived in Republika Srpska, and this Commander never issued me with an order to kill anyone. We were in charge of reconnaissance and intelligence activities. I was even praised by this one person when I let Mr. X, the witness, when I let him go, he told me that is what I should have done anyway. After that this Pelemis arrived in October and everything changed. The Unit was extended and some nationalists joined the Unit. It was horrible for me. It was a horrible experience for me. I will tell you exactly what happened. I could not do it yesterday but I can do it now. So Pelemis introduced himself and he said, "Well, I am your new Commander", and he said he was a hero of Republika Srpska. "OK, you are a hero. I am nobody, but that is fine with me". He said he was from the main staff, that he was working for the intelligence service and that we were to obey strictly his orders. Well, what was I supposed to do? I just kept silent, everybody else did. So after that I had been given my rank from the former Commander and Pelemis said, "OK, you can continue with your rank". He had heard that I was an honest man, that I was not a liar and so on. OK. I got my assignments. At that time I received a report which was to help me for that assignment. They had everything written down, the type of vehicles, the route to be taken and the description of the person we were supposed to arrest. They were even going to give us a helicopter for that kind of action. So I did not undertake anything before I checked it all myself, together with four other colleagues. So when I got there, when I got to the site, I realised that the report was not true. It was not true that it was not dangerous, because they were assuring me that the civilian population would not be harmed. That is what was stated in the report that I had been given which had been signed by Pelemis. So I sat down with my colleagues. I could talk to them. I knew them, and I told them, "Well, is this the kind of situation that we have seen? Is this what it says in the report? Can you see these people here in these meadows, women and children? They are Muslims. They do not care about fighting. They are just working on their fields in order to survive", and none of my soldiers ever pointed a gun at those Muslims and I do not think their names will ever appear before any Tribunal, thanks to me, because Pelemis would have exposed them to the same trouble I have been exposed to. So we came back from that assignment and I told them that the report was not true, and at that time I would like to emphasise that - I would like you to understand me, your Honours - at that time I was the Commander of the 1st Sabotage Unit which was part of the Bijeljina platoon. I am emphasising this because you have mentioned two of my refusals to carry out Pelemis's orders. Did you not mention that two times that I refused to carry out orders?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is for the Presiding Judge to put the questions, but to set your mind at rest, not only are we listening to you because you have been talking now for some twenty minutes, I believe, and none of the Judges interrupted you, normally it was the mitigating circumstances that we wanted to hear about, duress, threats, etc. We have let you speak. I would be happy to answer your question. Yes, I do believe we are listening to you and we are not interrupting you. So please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. So I went back to Bijeljina. I was debriefed and I had agreed with those four comrades who were all Serbs, and I was a Croat and I was the Commander of that Unit because I knew the area and that is why I had been given the assignment in the first place. So we agreed that the task could not be carried out because people could get killed, both members of the Muslim army, Muslim civilians and my colleague soldiers. I believe that none of us would have survived. So I went back. I reported to my superiors in writing. They probably asked those four colleagues whether what I had written was true. I do not know. Maybe Pelemis had his informant among those four people - who knows - because that is what kind of people the intelligence people are. However, they gave me their support. Several days later, Colonel Salapura arrived from the main intelligence centre and convened a meeting. So he had the floor and he knew that I had saved this witness X, but Pelemis did not know about that at that time. So Salapura tells me, "Mr. Erdemovic, what do you think, what kind of behaviour is that? Do you know who the Commander is here? Do you know who is in charge of issuing orders? What do you think? What kind of an attitude is that? You are a Commander. You should co-operate with the command not with your soldiers". I told him, "Well, I prefer my soldiers to you because you are sitting comfortably in your armchairs while we are freezing to death in mountains", and so he just looked at me, but that is what I told him. So he said,"OK, I know, you are lying. We have our people working for us. They have been informing us. We know what you have been doing". When he said "you," he meant Croats, because there were two Croats and one Slovenian there. I said, "OK, I am prepared to answer, to be accountable, for everything that I did". So I came to work the next day, because I was under a contract - I would like to emphasise that - I had a regular job. I had to be there at 7 o'clock and I worked until 3 o'clock in the afternoon in the barracks in Bijeljina. I could not move without permission. So that is when I was taken off my rank and that is when the abuse started. My wife gave birth in October, on 21st October. I had a very small child. My wife fell sick. It was winter and then later in March she was still sick and my son was still very small. So I kept sitting by his bed because I love him dearly and I was feeding him because my wife could not get up from bed, he was sick, and I had to go to work the next morning. I had to go to the barracks; I simply had to. Nobody asked me whether I wanted to, whether I could; I had to. So I had to leave my bedridden wife and my child. I had no time to eat myself. My small son was crying and, well, it is good that I still know what happened. So I went to the barracks and I had no time. I had not had time to shave. Pelemis was there, and he said, "Half of you are not - haven't shaved" and then Pelemis said, "Erdemovic, who are you trying to fuck here?" I apologise for this expression. He said, "You should be ashamed of yourself. You forgot to shave this morning and only yesterday you were in charge here, you were a Commander". I thought I was going to ask him to go home because my wife was sick, but then I realised that I could not ask for anything any more because I could even be sent to a prison. So, several days later we were sitting here, this friend of mine and myself, four of us, we were sitting in the corridor and talking, and Pelemis comes by and nobody stands up to greet him. He is an officer. We were supposed to stand up and greet him but nobody did. Then again, "You, Erdemovic", but then again, "You mother fucker" - I apologise once again - "Who do you think you are? Who do you really think you are?" I just kept silent. "Why don't you get up?" I said, "Well, my colleagues did not get up either". "You used to be their Commander. That is what you have taught him. You have just taught them disrespect for their superiors". I just kept silent. I thought it was just better for me not to say anything then, to talk. After that nothing, I did not have any contacts with Pelemis whatsoever. I only had contacts with this other Commander and Pelemis would not hear about me any more. He was not interested about me, but I knew that he was up to something. I knew that he was going to send me somewhere. I know that he would send some people to liquidate me. I was not 100 per cent sure, but I just had this feeling. This friend of mine mentioned me something to that effect. He was also a member of my Unit. Not only me, but many others, irrespective whether they were Serbs too, I will tell you about one of our actions. It was a covert action, and a Serb went to town and told his girlfriend something in connection with that Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 272 to 288. action, but then this girl, you know, you know women, they tell each other things, and the story went through town and, "Who said that?" and it was that man. You know what Mr. Pelemis said? "You go there. I do not care. You are going to enemy territory now. If your lives - if you lose your lives, then it is going to be his fault". But he did not tell anyone of the boys to kill that Serb. Fortunately, there was no shooting and this Serb was not killed, therefore. After that comes Srebrenica. I tell you, I came to work in the morning. The Commander of the platoon said, "Get ready, you are off to an assignment". So what could I do? I took my rifle and I went off to this assignment. I do not know where, only Pelemis knew and probably the Commander of the platoon. As I said, we came on 10th in the evening, I cannot tell, above the town of Srebrenica. It was the first time in my life that I had seen Srebrenica. Pelemis said, "OK, you are going to sleep there". We slept outdoors. We did not have anything. We slept on the ground. He went some place, probably to a bed. "I will come back tomorrow and I will issue your orders". I kept silent and I was not anything, and he was talking to the Commanders and I was not interested. I was no longer a Commander. In the morning he came and said that we had got orders to go to Srebrenica, to go down to Srebrenica as a Sabotage Unit and that we would be joined by some of the soldiers from the Drinski Corps, and that is the way it was. About 9.00, 9.30, I do not know exactly, we went down to a town. Of course they prepared us. They said that there would be heavy resistance and that there were, I do not know how many armed soldiers, and that they were extreme Muslims. That is what they explained. But we went into town. Not a single shot was fired at us, not a single bullet was shot at us. It was really strange to me. I was wondering, what is this? Where are these people? What is going on? We came to what I think was the centre of the town. I tried to explain this to Mr. Ruez. He probably checked that and he said it was the centre of the town. I thank him for that. Let it be known that I am not lying. Nothing - our orders were to stop, not to go anywhere before General Mladic would come. Pelemis said, "Drazen" - no, not to me, he told somebody else, "Take four men and go back to the southern part". Ruez helped us tell which side this was, where this was. "When General Mladic comes into town, let us know by radio communication that he is entering town". From then onwards I have no idea what happened in Srebrenica and elsewhere. I saw some of it on BBC, here on television, and I talked about this with the investigating gentleman. He asked me about certain details in connection with these films. I told him what I knew and what I did not know, I did not know, but when I saw those people in the camp I was really surprised. How could that happen, that I could be there and not see these people? I do not know. I wondered myself. I probably do not know why. That is the way it was. We spent the night - that night in Srebrenica. Pelemis came again the next day and he said, "We are packing up, we are going. There is nothing else to be done. Our assignment has been completed." OK, fine. We all crowded into our vehicles and went back to our homes. Then, of course, in the vehicle we would talk and I asked a man from Vlasenica, "What is going on? Where are these people? Is this the Srebrenica that was surrounded for four years?" He said, "I do not know. I do not know". That is what he said. After that, while travelling, I told you our vehicle broke down and we were left behind for a long time until it was repaired. When we came to the base of the Vlasenica platoon, we heard about Pelemis causing a traffic accident which killed a soldier who was in the group that I had commanded previously. Tomorrow, the next day, when we got up, Pelemis did not tell me personally, but a man who was in - who was part of the quartermaster's Corps, he told me that something should be bought for this man's family and he said, "You are going and four more people were going". I said, "Of course, I liked this man. He never said anything bad do me. He never said that I was Croat and that he was a Serb or that he hated me". On the contrary, they always went to the place where I lived so that we would have coffee together or what I would have, if I had something else for us to drink. Of course, I will tell you now while I was in Bijeljina - I forgot that - my next door neighbour was Muslim. We were on friendly terms and this man helped me cure my son once because he was running a high fever and he gave me a natural syrup made of apples which would reduce a fever, and I did not smoke at the time and I would give this man who was an elderly man in his 60s, perhaps, I would give him these cigarettes that I had received. I was also in touch with these girls, these two friends, (redacted) (redacted) . These two girls were Muslims also. Nothing whatever happened. They came to my son's first birthday party and they bought him the most valuable of presents. I can never forget that, a gold bracelet. I do not know why - perhaps because I was bad or perhaps because I was good. Even now they are sending their regards to me and I thank them for it. Now let me go on once again what happened. When I came back from the funeral on 16th in the morning, I tell you Pelemis did not tell me directly but Brano Gojkovic came and said, "Erdemovic, Kos Franc and Goronja Zoran, get ready. You going on to a mission". So what could we do? I asked when we would be going home. He said, "You are going on a mission. What kind of a home are you talking about?" So I had to go on this mission, I had to. I did not know, but I did not know what it was. Had I known what it was, I would not have moved from there. They would have to kill me on the spot. I do not know what. Had I been the Commander of the group, then I tell you, quite frankly, I would have refused that assignment with an explanation, I will try to find an explanation for the command; I would have tried. I will tell what you this explanation would have been. I would have said that this was a crime, that this is punishable and I would have primarily persuaded my colleagues that people are held accountable for that kind of thing, that this is not a minor affair, that people lose their lives. That is how I would explain this. Then they would help me when I would report to Pelemis. They would defend me. But I was not Commander then, regrettably. An idiot was Commander, an idiot - not a fool, an idiot. A fool is good and honest, but an idiot is an idiot. We came to Zvornik. He reported to this command, to a Lieutenant Colonel. I do not know his name or surname and I saw his rank, his insignia on his chest. This Lieutenant Colonel told our driver, "Sit in the vehicle and follow me", and that is the way it was. We were driven off to this farm. Again this Lieutenant Colonel was talking to Brano saying - I do not know what they were talking about, I do not know, I was not present during that conversation. When this Lieutenant Colonel sat in the vehicle and started going away, then Brano said, "Now buses will be brought in with civilian population from Srebrenica, men." He emphasised civilians, that is to say, that they would be wearing civilian clothes. I said, "People, I do not want this, are you normal?" Nothing. "Mr. Erdemovic" - this is what Brano told me - "if you do not want to, stand with them so that I, so that we can kill you too or give them weapons so that they can shoot you". I was not afraid for myself at that point, not that much. If I were alone, I would have run away, I would have tried to do something, just as they tried to flee into the forest or whatever. But what would happen to my child and to my wife? So there was this enormous burden falling on my shoulders. On the one hand, I knew that I would be killing people, that I could not hide this, that this would be burning at my conscience. I cannot bring up my child if I conceal things like that. How can I bring up my child properly and teach him good things if I am hiding something that is bad, that is a crime? Then, on the other hand, how can I sacrifice my child which was only a few months old and my wife, and they were not to be blamed for anything. So I was in this Unit, so I had a guilty conscience in terms of myself. So what do I do? If I sacrifice myself and my family, again it would be the same; these people would be killed again because I am not deciding on their fate. So, as I said, what happened happened. I saw that I had no way out, and I had to shoot these people. I tried to refuse. I tried to explain, "People, people are held accountable for this. Do you know what you are doing?" No, they probably did not have the kind of conscience I had. Let me tell you, none of them had families so that was probably the reason too. They did not think about this very much. But then all of a sudden it became clear in my head. What was I supposed to do? Where do I go? Before I could run to one town and then another town or whatever. Where do I go with a wife and with a small child? Where? Where? What happened happened; buses started coming in. There were two military policemen escorting these buses. They would bring out groups of 10 people out of the bus and, of course, they were looking into the ground. I remember the first bus. I remember the first bus. Their heads were bent downwards and their hands were tied and they were blindfolded. I remember the first bus, but all the rest is dimmed, as I told Mr. Ruez. I do not know. Doctors, when they talked to me, when doctors talked to me, they asked me, "Drazen, perhaps out of this fear of yours, out of this psychological thing, I mean, all the things that you lived through, experienced, did you say that there were 20 buses, that there were so many people?" I said, "People", I said that many because that is the way it seemed to me and I think that is the way it was. I did not count them, nor did I think it was right to count, but I think that that is how it was. If you look at the time that all of this had taken, it all fits into this mosaic. After that, later, I do not know what time it was, these people from Bratunac came and not all of them had even gotten out of their vehicles, and I showed Mr. Ruez one of them. You can see this on BBC television on their films. This man was probably born in Srebrenica and he was in the Bratunac Brigade and he was a Serb. He said, "Ah, ah, you, Turk, you were the worst one in Srebrenica. You did this, you did that". They started beating them. I do not know what they were doing to people. I cannot describe this. I do not have the words to do that. Nothing. Nothing. I just kept quiet, kept quiet. I tried to save a man. I had certain arguments because he saved Serbs who were in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This man was giving their telephone numbers to have this checked, but there were no witnesses. The command was all should be dead and no witnesses. I did not even know when the end would come. Then this Lieutenant Colonel came in and he used the following words, "In the hall in Pilica there were 500 people", so the figure he used is the figure I used, 500. Then I had really broken down, you know, as we say in Yugoslavia, broken down. That means that I was distressed, psychologically, physically, I do not know what, and I said I would not do it any more. I do not know why I decided then that I would not do it, I do not know, I do not know, I am not aware of that, but had - he said that I would have to do it, and probably I was supported by some of my comrades. That is why I was so resolute perhaps, I do not know, I do not know exactly. Had he said that I had to do it, I would have turned my rifle towards him and I would have shot him. "If you say that I have to do it, well, I do not have to do it" and I would have done that, no matter what happened to me after that at that point. But afterwards I was afraid. The next few days I was wondering, what had I done. I was afraid. I was afraid that they would try to liquidate me because of my behaviour at that farm. I refused that. These comrades supported me and after that we went to this meeting. Nothing important was said there. We went back to Vlasenica and we came to Bijeljina. I kept saying, "Please, let us go home". Some individuals were already drunk. They were saying, "Wait, wait, wait, let's have another drink." I said, "Come on, people, let's go home. I want to go see my child". Fortunately, fortunately, I said, the Lieutenant Colonel said that we could go. God knows when we would have left there. I came to Bijeljina. I came home, as I said. I was in a hurry to go home to see my wife and child. I know what I had experienced and all of that hurt, but what could I do? I did not want anything. I did not want the war. I did not want that, but what could I do? I kept quiet. I could not tell my wife about what had happened. I was worried how to put them away some place. I knew what Pelemis had been doing to me before that, and now what will he do now? However, not much time had gone by and what I had expected came true. My colleague shot three bullets at me and two other friends. Why, I do not know. The authorities of Republika Srpska had carried out this investigation and, of course, the owner of this cafe had reported the shooting because he had to do it for his own safety. He was interrogated and all the witnesses and they all corroborated the same story, because these two witnesses were in better condition than I was. I could not speak because of the consequences of the wounding. Only some 20 days after that I was visited by these inspectors from Bijeljina in Belgrade at the military hospital. "Drazen, what happened? Are you going to tell us about it?" "People, I cannot tell you about it. I am afraid. I cannot tell you anything. Are you going to bring charges?" "How do I bring charges? He tried to kill me the other day." I kept quiet. The Muslim was also asked and he said: "No, no, nothing. No, no, no, forget it." I remembered but I said: "No, no, this was forgotten. How do I know who would tell who what?" When I left the hospital, ah yes, in the hospital I was only visited by one man from my unit, only one man from my unit. He also lived in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and he helped me stay alive, rather have me transported from Bijeljina to the military hospital in Belgrade. He explained some other details to me, then what was being done, what would happen. He advised me to move my family away. I had been wounded so badly that I had been operated on and this stoma was removed only in the Netherlands. But when I came home I was wounded. I did not have a single dinar, not a single dinar. The medicine was exorbitant, the medicine I needed was exorbitant. Had it not been for some people who I had known who had cafes and who knew I was a good man and also some companies, had I not asked them for money for my medicine nobody would have given it to me. I would have died. There were no medicaments at the Bijeljina hospital and all of this is privately owned, pharmacies, everything. To tell you exactly, the only pharmacy in Belgrade that had my medicines and those stoma and other things I needed cost 150 deutschemarks and this was only to last me for 20 days, only 20 days. So wounded as I was, I would take the bus and go to Belgrade to buy my medicine. When I would come to the border, I want to say that too, between Republika Srpska and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as far as I could see, these policemen behaved towards me in a humane manner. They never asked me, "What are you doing Croat? Where do you want to go? What are you doing?" They would always say, "Sir, would you please show us your papers? Where you are going?" I would show my permit, they would have a look at it, and then I would do the same thing that I did yesterday. I would raise my shirt and they would see the wounds, the stoma and they would say, "Fine". "I am just going to buy this medicine I need and I am going back immediately." After that I wondered: How could I transfer my wife and where do I transfer her? Problems again. I was being threatened. In the street they were saying loud and clear, "You're an Ustasha." Although I was in their army I was an Ustasha for them. My wife was Ustasha hoar for them because she had borne a Croat child. That is the kind of people they are. Why? Why, because Pelemis had talked them into that. I suffered. I suffered. I had the strength to sustain all of that. Fortunately, IFOR came into Bosnia. Routes were being opened Orasje and Tuzla, the road between Oraci and Tuzla, going by the town of Brcko and I besieged my wife and child. I could not tell her what happened. She had assumed what had happened. She knew I was wounded and I said, "Please, you and the child go there, go to our parents, so that you would stay alive at least and it does not matter what happens to me. Please just take my child away." I had such trouble talking her into it. She was wondering whether she would run into problems with the Muslim authorities there. I said: "Don't be afraid, (redacted). The people from the Muslim Ministry of the Interior know me. They know that I am not that kind of person. They know everything about me. They have my files. They know that I am not a criminal, that I never committed a crime. I did not even fight with anybody or quarrel with anybody, nothing." Then she agreed. A friend of mine, a Serb, drove her there by car, my wife and child, they went to Tuzla. I came back to Bijeljina. Then when I got out of this friend's car I did not know what to do. Where do I go now? I know the next day when people would find out that my wife went to Tuzla it would all be over. I was suspected even then. Then after that what could I do? I knew what had destroyed my life and that is what troubled me. First, I was wondering whether I should commit suicide, take five kilograms of explosives tied around me, walk into the office of Milorad Pelemis and blow him up and myself. It would be of no use. Where is the truth there? What is the truth about Drazen Erdemovic? Why did Drazen Erdemovic have to go through all of that and why did he have to live through such things? I was talking to a friend and he said, "Drazen, Salapura and Mico are not worthy of your life. Do something else. Don't do that." I listened to that man and I did what I did. I went to a friend in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I thought of getting in touch with you directly, the International Tribunal, but I did not have any contact. I did not have a passport. I only had an ID from Tuzla, this military contract, and an ID stating the unit I belonged to. No other documents. Also this green card. I do not have if I have it here. I do not know. I told this friend of mine about this, you know, and he looked at me and he said: "You're crazy." I said: "Yes, I am crazy." I said: "Yes, you are with your child." I looked at his child and I said: "Where is (redacted)"? Why? I do not know why. I know actually what happened but I do not know why. Why did all of this happen. I said resolutely that is what I have decided. I shall either be dead or I shall tell about what I know before the International Tribunal. Then this friend of mine understood what I was saying and helped me get in touch with journalists. Without any guesswork involved I told this lady journalist, I said that I was not asking for any money or for any services from her, any favours. I just asked her to help me get to The Hague. I asked her: "Please, don't let this be revealed. If it is revealed I am a dead man. It is not that I will be a dead man, it is not that that is important. I took part in this. I feel guilty because of that. I feel some kind of guilt, but this man who helped me and I am staying with him, he is not to be blamed and he will suffer because of that and his child will suffer." Not even two days had gone by since I gave this interview my friend and I were arrested. We were arrested by the State Security of the Republic of Serbia. They did not beat us up or anything. They did not torture us in any way. They knew everything about me. They simply took away the lady's cassette at the airport in Belgrade. They had everything. I know that they have everything. This lady told me and this friend of mine it is all over. I was searched at Belgrade airport and the cassette was taken away. Nothing. I said: "What do I do now with my friend?" I look at his wife and child and I say: "God, if I destroy my own life, OK, but what do I do with this man?" Nothing. After this call, after less than half an hour, the police knocked at the door. They said it was the police and nothing. They opened the door. They walked in. They said nicely: "Take your jackets, put your shoes on and come with us." Nothing. My friend and I got up and left. Of course, we could not talk to each other. I was looking at one side. He was looking to the other side. We came to this place, the SUP, the Ministry of the Interior and then interrogation started. He was in one room. I was in another room. Nobody had harassed me in any way. One man told me though that I was a Croat spy, but then he was intoxicated. I said, OK, I helped Serbs in Tuzla and I am married to a Serb. I do not know what I had said and he looked at me. A pleasant man came, I must say just as pleasant as Mr. Ruez who talked to me. He was fair and decent. I knew then that they had everything and that they knew everything and I knew why they arrested me. It started and I told them everything just as I told you, everything, everything, all the details, all the details. I said that I was forced to do that. I was not afraid that they would arrest some of the people who were there with me. Let them arrest them and let any one of them say I was not forced to do that. I told these people all of that and this man believed me, and they would not even handcuff me after that, me or my friend. We were not in prison in Novi Sad, no, that is to not true. We were on Dedinje in a house that was guarded by the State Security of the Republic Serbia. I was not harassed in any way. They provided medicine for me for my wounds. I had fruit, food just like I have here in detention and also a fair attitude. I was treated fairly. I was not addressed by "hey, you spy" by these men who were with me. They probably received orders from their superiors. Oh yes, and then I appeared before this court in Novi Sad. Then Mr. Jovan Babic became my attorney. I just looked at this man and I saw that he was an honest man, an honest man. I just looked at him. I asked him what I should do and he said: "Drazen, the best thing for you is to say the truth, exactly what had happened and how it had happened." Then I told the whole story again before the court in Novi Sad. Mr. Jovan Babic put certain questions that he thought were unclear. He asked me about all these armies, because it is a bit unusual to everyone, how come I was in three armies. So that is why I had to speak about this at length. I told the whole story. I even said the name of the man who was supposed to transfer me to Switzerland. I do not know if that is in the papers that came in from Yugoslavia, but I think that the name is there. They asked me and I told them the name. Mr. Ruez did not ask me and whatever he had asked me I answered. So that is how it happened. My counsel told me that we would be seeing each other every week. The first time we met I asked him - I actually gave him a telephone number and I asked him to contact that person and to get some news of my wife, my son and the rest of my family in Tuzla because I knew that they had heard everything, that that they had heard about my statement. He told me: "Drazen, don't you worry about that. It has been taken care of. I had just said that and he told me that it had all been taken care of. The next time we saw each other he told me: "Your family is OK." I told him: "Well, don't lie to me. Tell me openly what's going on with them?" He said: "They are fine. They are doing fine. You should not worry about anything." So then this procedure started and gentlemen whose names I do not remember from the Tribunal came. They talked to me, not for very long. They just asked me whether I was willing to come to The Hague. I said to the Security Services that I wanted to go to The Hague. That is what I also told the court in Novi Sad and that is what I am telling you now. That is how it all happened. That is how I arrived here on 30th March. Then the proceedings that you are aware of started. Yesterday I told you about that. The Prosecution and my Defence counsel told you how much I helped the Prosecution and they said that yesterday. I do not think I should repeat that here again.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine, Mr. Erdemovic. Please return to your usual seat. We are going to proceed to a recess, unless there are any questions? Mr. Babic, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: No. I think that the testimony has been given in detail and that his personality can be seen.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I think, your Honour, we have one question to Mr. Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, you have read and heard the facts stated in this indictment many, many times. I am certain that you realise that there is one crucial question to which the Court needs to have an absolute clear answer. That is, from the moment on 16th July 1995 when you realised what your task was going to be and until around 3 o'clock in the afternoon when the shooting stopped, did you at any point have any possibility to avoid taking part in this shooting without jeopardising your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, that is my most sincere and frank answer; not because I am defending myself. I am really being honest. First, you may remember yesterday you mentioned, I did not mention, I did not even know that, that the crime was actually discovered by me and you had not been aware of that crime before that.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Your answer to this crucial question is no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. MR. OSTBERG: Thank you. No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Judge Odio Benito?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, could you tell us how your relationship was with your parents when you were a kid in Tuzla, a kid and a young boy? How was your relationship with your family in general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How shall I put it? The relations were good, at least I think they were good. I did not spend much time with my father who was away in business very often in various towns in Yugoslavia. He would leave Tuzla for Serbia, for a town in Serbia or in Croatia, for his work. That was the kind of work he had. So I spent much more time with my mother. To be honest, I was relatively free. They did not force me to do anything. They taught me not to hate anyone. I am grateful for that to them. They taught me to be a law-abiding person. Even when my dad was at home when, for example, some older friends would come and ask for me to go to a party, my father trusted those friends of mine who were older than myself and he told them: "You will be responsible for him." So it was quite free. I was not made to do anything. They did not tell me to do this or that. There was not such a thing.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Are your parents still alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When you were wounded in the hospital in Belgrade, did you receive their visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you, I was only visited by this friend, a colleague from my unit, and I was also visited once by my wife and my child throughout that one month period.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Do you know why they did not visit you, your parents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was impossible for them to travel from Tuzla to Belgrade. It was impossible to reach Belgrade at that time. The roads were not opened and IFOR was not yet there. Only the UN forces were there in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You told us during your declaration this morning that at sometime you were transferred near to Vukovar. When id this happen, when you were transferred to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not in Vukovar. I was in a place some 15 kilometres away from Vukovar. There was a checkpoint there and it was while I was doing my regular military service with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When in 1991, in the summer of '91. I do not recall the exact date but it was in July, I believe. I do not know exactly. I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Before these Srebrenica facts had you killed anyone in the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That is why I have been tormented by that so much when I have to talk about it. That was the first and the last time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, just one question. Your future depends of course on what the Tribunal is going to decide, but when you foresee your own future how do you see things in terms of your family life, professional life, in social terms, geographical terms? How do you see your future?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I have been discussing it with doctors, the doctors who have been suggested by the Tribunal. They asked me - at the beginning you knew how I was. I started to cry during my initial appearance and everything. So while I was talking to them I kept telling them that my life had been destroyed and that my life was worthless, but later on these guards in the detention unit helped me. They would beg me to get out to do some sport, to do something, you know, just to keep those thoughts away. So I started to react positively. I started playing table tennis. Although I was still wounded I was trying to play basketball, you know, I had to. I felt I should do it because those people, one of them, he can speak Yugoslavian and he told me: "Drazen, why are you doing this to yourself? You are here but you are not alone." So he tried to convince, well, he was doing his job. I know he is a guard there. Then the doctors paid me another visit and we talked again and they asked me: "Drazen, how are you doing now?" I told them: "Well, thank God I am doing fine. This surgery has been performed. My wife had visited me with my child. The guards are behaving in a very correct way. I have not been forced to do anything. My lawyer also cheers me up when he comes to see me. We make jokes." I told them I was feeling much better, but I still had those thoughts. I am still asking myself why I am not together with my wife and my child, with my parents. Why has all this happened? Why am I here? Why have I become a criminal? Why am I in a prison? Why? Why? All because of others. Others did this to me. Of course I have to be tormented by that. Of course I have to think about what happened on that farm. I have to have those thoughts because I lost everything. I have lost all my friends. OK, I have not lost the real friends, they are sending their regards, even some Muslim friends because they do not believe, even some people who are in important positions in Tuzla, who work for the Ministry of the Interior, they are just saying that this is not possible that I would do this of my own free will. The Commander of my unit in the Muslim army who is a Muslim by nationality, he said: "No, that is not Drazen Erdemovic. That is not him." The Commander of my HVO unit also: "No, no, that is not Drazen Erdemovic. We know Drazen Erdemovic very well." They keep sending their regards, my friends. On 21st October some of them came to my son's birthday party and there were Muslims, Serbs and Croats there and I could not be there. Why? Because of this Pelemis, because of Salapura, because of the war, because of everything, because of everything.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I believe Judge Riad has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, in your long description of your life you have not mentioned anything about your profession. Could you tell us something about your profession, before the war at least? A. Yes, I have mentioned that. I am a locksmith by occupation. I graduated from secondary, vocational secondary school in Tuzla in 1989. There was no work at that time in former Yugoslavia. It was very difficult to find a job. I did not have any money to pay to get a job. People who did not have any money, they were just supposed to wait and keep quiet. I was not employed at all. At that time the conflicts in the former Yugoslavia started and everything stopped at that time. Factories no longer worked, nothing. Q. You were very clear in expressing to us your belief in the co-existence of all religious and racial factions in ex-Yugoslavia, and you pleaded very much the cause of peace. At the same time you happened to join all the fighting groups during this war. Was there not any other way to express your belief in co-existence? A. How shall I put it? We were forced to join the army. I had received these call-up papers. I had no one to turn to. Who was I? I was just simple Drazen Erdemovic with nobody who would listen to me. I could not go to see a President or a Commander of a unit. I told you that this morning. I did not vote for either the SDS, HDZ or SDA. I voted for the reformists, Mr. Ante Markovic's party who won in Tuzla. I did not vote for nationalists such as Beslagic in Tuzla, but nobody was interested to know that. Nobody said: "Drazen Erdemovic, you did not vote for any nationalist party. You are against the war." No. "Drazen, go to the war. Willy-nilly, you have to go too."

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: According to your observation during this period, was this the case of all the young people of your age in former Yugoslavia? Did they all have to pass through this ordeal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I will tell you this. Some, for example people who were older than myself, they had a passport, but my generation, for example, we did not have a passport. We were minor at that time. Before you do your military service and if your parents did not work abroad you could not get a passport, such was the law at that time. You simply could not have a passport before you do your military service. Once you have done your military service you can make a request to be issued a passport and then they would do some checks, checking your record and then they would issue you a passport. But before I completed my military service the war broke out. So, who was supposed to issue me a passport? That was the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I was asking the Registrar to make sure it might not be necessary to make some corrections or erasures in some of the indications that were very personal that appeared or that were stated during the testimony which might cause anybody to be insecure about anything. It is now 1.30. We are going to adjourn the session. I want to thank the interpreters who have worked very hard. We will not begin until 3.15. The Court stands adjourned. We will resume at a quarter after 3. (1.30 p.m.) (3.15 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Would you please have the accused brought in? In accordance with what we said this morning, we will first hear the closing remarks of the Prosecutor, the argument of the Defence, and for a very short statement that he might want to make without his having to take an oath, we will hear the accused. But before I give the floor to the Prosecutor, I would first like to point out a point of the proceedings against Drazen Erdemovic in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In my hands I have a decision which was taken on 29th May 1996 by the Trial Court II presided over by Mrs. MacDonald in which the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia's government was requested to transmit to the International Tribunal the facts of the investigation and, if necessary, a copy of the case files of the judgment of its national courts. This morning Mr. Babic submitted to us the Novi Sad court decision which will be translated. I shall turn to the Prosecutor's Office and ask if you have those documents? If you do, can they be annexed to the other documents in the proceedings? You have the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I see no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: They can be annexed. You have no objection to their being annexed. Does the Defence object to that? The Registrar will contact the Trial Chamber to make sure which parts of the documents should be translated. Without any further ado, I once again give the floor to the Prosecution so that he can make his closing remarks in this case. I give you the floor, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Before the final arguments which are going to be given by Mr. Harmon, if it pleases the Court, I would like to briefly address the question of venue for a prison sentence, if prison is imposed by the Court. We have not taken up this issue before. The Registrar has filed with the Trial Chamber and also sent copies to the Defence, I believe, and to the Prosecutor's Office discussing where could a prison sentence be executed. I have gone through the memorandum from the Registrar and eleven countries have declared their willingness to execute prison sentences by this Tribunal. However, four of them, Denmark, Netherlands, Germany and Sweden, have restricted their willingness to accept convicted nationals only of residents of those respective states. The Netherlands, Denmark, Germany and Sweden can then not be in question. Croatia which, in the report of the Secretary-General, is said not to be a place to execute prison sentences. No State from the former Yugoslavia should, in the view of the Secretary-General, take on them to execute prison sentences. Others on this list, Iran and Pakistan, have not adopted a specific legislation to do this. That leaves us with three States, namely, Finland, Norway and Italy. In the opinion of the Prosecutor's Office, we have no preference as to which one of these three possible States imprisonment would take place. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prosecutor. I will perhaps not give the floor to the Defence immediately on this point. I think that Mr. Babic will have the opportunity to say what he has to say about that point during his final arguments. Do you agree, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Harmon, representing the Office of the Prosecutor, for the closing remarks, I now give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honours. The defendant before you, Mr. Drazen Erdemovic, will be the first person to be sentenced for war crimes before an International Criminal Tribunal in 50 years. Mr. Erdemovic has pleaded guilty to a crime against humanity, the underlying facts of which are undisputed and which involve the mass murder by a firing squad of 1200 defenceless men and boys from Srebrenica. This crime was one of enormous proportions and, by his own admissions, Mr. Erdemovic's role in it was significant. He has stated at various times to various people that he killed between 10 and 100 people. Exactly how many people Mr. Erdemovic personally killed on 16th July 1995, I cannot tell you. I do not know. Mr. Erdemovic may not know and you will never know; only God knows. But what I am certain of is that the massacre at Branjevo farm was amongst the largest crimes committed during the tragic conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that Mr. Erdemovic's deadly actions contributed to it. However reluctantly he says was his participation in it, he did so throughout the day. When not engaged in the killings, his presence at the scene armed with an automatic weapon undoubtedly assisted in creating an atmosphere of fear and intimidation wherein countless victims walked to their deaths rather than attempt to resist or to flee. The facts behind the charges against Mr. Erdemovic have in all respects been corroborated by the investigations of the Office of the Prosecutor. In every national jurisdiction, the taking of a life or of lives by another is punishable by the severest of sanctions, often by imprisonment up to and including a life term or, in some national jurisdictions, by death. In this case the maximum punishment which Mr. Erdemovic faces is a life imprisonment term. Were Mr. Erdemovic one who planned, organised or instigated this monstrous crime or took significant initiative in it, my recommendation to you would be simple and direct, impose a life sentence. That will not be my recommendation to you. In deciding upon the proper sentence in this case, the Trial Chamber must be guided by Articles 24.2 and 7.4 of the Statute of the Tribunal and Rule 101 of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, all of which set forth factors that the Trial Chamber shall consider in imposing a proper sentence. The relevant factors mentioned in those provisions include the gravity of the offence and the individual circumstances of the convicted person, whether the accused was following superior orders, any aggravating circumstances, any mitigating circumstances, the substantial co-operation with the Prosecutor by the convicted person and the general practice regarding prison sentences in the courts of the former Yugoslavia. In respect of aggravating and mitigating circumstances, the Prosecutor's Office has filed a brief with the Trial Chamber on this subject. What makes this case particularly difficult is finding the proper balance between punishing Mr. Erdemovic for the aggravated crime of which he stands convicted and giving recognition to the considerable factors in mitigation which are also present in his case. I have already discussed the aggravating circumstances of this case, the slaughter of 1200 defenceless men and boys over a five hour time period on a single day and Mr. Erdemovic's role in it constitutes an aggravating factor. I need not repeat myself in this regard. I would, however, like to address some of the factors of mitigation that the Prosecutor considers relevant for your deliberations. The first of these concerns the actions taken by Mr. Erdemovic to surrender himself to the Tribunal. As this Chamber is aware, Mr. Erdemovic attempted to travel to The Hague in order to confess his guilt but en route was arrested by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. He was later transferred to The Hague at our request. Until Mr. Erdemovic took affirmative steps to self-surrendering, he was like one of the faceless, nameless executioners depicted in Goya's famous painting, The Executions of May 3rd, and he would have remained so had he not voluntarily set into motion a chain of events that brought him before the Tribunal. Until he made those efforts, the Prosecutor neither knew of him, nor of the killing fields at Branjevo farm, nor of the execution site at the cultural hall in Pilica. Shortly after being transferred to The Hague Mr. Erdemovic met with Mr. Jean Rene Ruez of the Prosecutor's Office and confessed to his crimes. After being indicted by the Prosecutor, he made his initial appearance before your Honours and accepted responsibility for his crimes by entering a guilty plea. During my and Office of the Prosecutor investigators' contacts with Mr. Erdemovic, he has expressed remorse for his actions of July 16th 1995. This combination of factors, his efforts to surrender himself to the Tribunal, his confession of guilt, his expressed remorse for his conduct and his prompt acceptance of responsibility for his crimes by pleading guilty are, in the Prosecutor's view, mitigating circumstances which we urge this honourable Trial Chamber to consider in determining a proper sentence. Another mitigating factor which the Trial Chamber may wish to consider is found in Article 7.4 of the Statute. Article 7.4 says that an accused person acting pursuant to an order of a superior shall not relieve him of criminal responsibility but may be considered in mitigation of punishment if the Tribunal determines that justice so requires. In this case, Mr. Erdemovic, a low ranking member of the Bosnian Serb Army, followed orders, albeit patently illegal orders, of a superior to execute innocent civilians. He says he did so out of fear for his life. You may consider these as mitigating circumstances and give them weight, whatever weight you deem appropriate. Rule 101(B)(ii) of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence explicitly provides that in determining the sentence, the Trial Chamber shall take into account, and I quote, "the substantial co-operation with the Prosecutor by the convicted person before or after conviction". Let me be very clear on this point. Mr. Erdemovic has provided substantial assistance to the Prosecutor's Office in relation to the investigations of Srebrenica. His co-operation was and continues to be voluntary and unconditional. By "unconditional" I mean that no promises were made to him by the Office of the Prosecutor to secure his co-operation and assistance. I would like to summarise for you the substantial nature of his assistance. As a result of his co-operation, the Office of the Prosecutor was informed for the first time about four criminal events. The first of those events occurred on July 11th 1995 and it involved the summary execution of a Bosnian Muslim civilian in Srebrenica. He provided us, secondly, with details about a summary execution of a Muslim prisoner in Vlasenica that was another war crime. Thirdly, he provided details about Branjevo farm in Pilica where 1200 civilians were murdered. Until Mr. Erdemovic informed us of this site, the Office of the Prosecutor was unaware of its existence. As a result of identifying this location, this past summer exhumations were conducted at the site and the remains of between 140 and 160 victims were recovered. These remains were mistakenly left at the site when the Bosnian-Serb Army attempted to cover up its crimes in September 1995. Steps are now underway to identify those victims whose remains were recovered and reunite them with their grieving families. Fourthly, Mr. Erdemovic provided details about the cultural hall in Pilica where an estimated 500 civilians were murdered. Until Mr. Erdemovic informed us of this site, the Office of the Prosecutor was unaware of its existence. Thereafter, investigators from my Office travelled to Pilica, located this site and conducted forensic examinations, the preliminary results of which confirm relevant aspects of Mr. Erdemovic's information. In addition to each of those criminal events, Mr. Erdemovic has provided us with the names and identities of many of the perpetrators responsible for these foul deeds. Simply put, without his assistance we would never have known or may never have known of their identities. His co-operation, in addition, has provided the Office of the Prosecutor with valuable information about the Drina Corps and about the structure of the Bosnian-Serb Army. As you may recall, your Honours, from the large map, Exhibit No. 1, and the location of the Pilica farm and the Branjevo, in the hall, in the cultural hall, in Pilica, your Honours are aware that those areas are far north of the other areas that were at the time known to the Office of the Prosecutor. In essence, the information provided by Mr. Erdemovic expanded the geographic range in which these killings took place and corroborate other evidence that the Office of the Prosecutor has showing that the executions of civilians from Srebrenica was well-planned, systematic and organised. This past summer, your Honours, Mr. Erdemovic testified at the Rule 61 hearing for Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic. I have submitted to your Honours in Exhibits 14 and 15 transcripts of Mr. Erdemovic's testimony at that particular hearing. As this Trial Chamber is aware, witnesses are often reluctant to testify publicly, yet Mr. Erdemovic, to his credit, when asked to testify at the Rule 61 hearing had no such hesitation and did so willingly. His testimony at the Rule 61 hearing was significant in two respects: Firstly, it contributed to this Trial Chamber's decision to issue international arrest warrants for Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic. Secondly, Mr. Erdemovic was the first Bosnian Serb Army insider to provide public testimony about the events at Srebrenica. His testimony exposed the lies of Bosnian-Serb political and military leaders that the killings of civilians from Srebrenica was nothing but Muslim propaganda. I would submit to your Honours that his testimony at the Rule 61 hearing influenced, in a positive sense, the public clamour to arrest Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic. In respect of both his co-operation with the Prosecutor and his decision to testify publicly at the Rule 61 hearings, these were courageous decisions by Mr. Erdemovic. I will tell your Honours quite frankly, his assistance to us has been invaluable. It has significantly advanced our investigations. I dare say that if the Office of the Prosecutor had the assistance of others like Mr. Erdemovic, our investigations would be considerably advanced. We believe that the substantial co-operation provided by Mr. Erdemovic to the Prosecutor's Office merits a significant mitigation of his sentence. Lastly, I would like to turn to Rule 101(B)(iii) which states that Trial Chamber shall take into account, and I quote, "the general practice regarding prison sentences in the courts of the former Yugoslavia". In our analysis of the laws of the former Yugoslavia, we believe that the crime entitled "War crimes against the civilian population" most closely resembles the crime for which Mr. Erdemovic stands convicted. In the former Yugoslavia this crime was punishable by a term of imprisonment between five and 20 years. If there were circumstances in mitigation, the minimum term could be reduced below five years. Now turning to the sentence in this case. The maximum sentence that this honourable Court may impose is a term of life imprisonment. Justice would not be served by imposing that sentence on Mr. Erdemovic, and we strongly urge the Court not to do so. Because of the considerable factors in mitigation which I have discussed, the Prosecutor recommends leniency in the case of Mr. Erdemovic. If it is the decision of this honourable Court to impose a term of imprisonment, we would respectfully recommend that it not exceed 10 years. Thank you very much, your Honours. That concludes my remarks.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Prosecution. I now give the floor to you, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, gentlemen, counsel for the Prosecution, after the accused Erdemovic pleaded guilty, at first it seemed that the proceedings would be simplified from that point on and that the only thing that remained was to pronounce the sentence. Is that the case? My answer has been and is a strong "no". The reason is that so many questions posed in the proceedings require an answer that would be rooted in the logic of every day and legally acceptable before any sentence can be pronounced. The hearing yesterday and the hearing today confirmed that and I will explain that in my closing argument. When I first contemplated the defence of the accused Erdemovic, sitting in my office I silently and somehow automatically scanned the titles of books in my library. My eyes lingered and my mind came awake at the title: "The naked and the dead." This is a novel that you will know, a novel by the American author, Norman Mailer; a book that paints a hardened up picture of war, a book in which the writer empathises with the fate of the soldiers, their relations, the atmosphere of fear, suffering and death. This is a book about the circumstances that have forced men to cause harm to each other and to themselves, a book in which man is but a victim. But this is also a book filled with yearning for the warmth and peaceful sleep without suffering blood, mud and insomnia. The title of the book summarises its content, the naked and the dead. The title reminded me forcibly of the fate of men in a cruel war in the former Yugoslavia. The fate of the dead and the fate of the naked. The fate of my client. That is why this title has from the start been a motto of my defence and the motto of this closing argument. It was a moral and professional stimulus to agree to defend the man accused of a grave crime, but the man who is also a victim of the whirlwind of war and the victim of his own deed. In the proceedings so far I did not dwell on that that much because everything was clear at the very first hearing of this Trial Chamber, of this Tribunal, in the presence of the accused Erdemovic, before the eyes of the world and the TV cameras. I am convinced, your Honours and my learned colleagues from the Prosecution, that even now after all this time you still feel the impact of the most poignant moment of the hearing. This is why I urge that the accused Erdemovic, because of his bad health and damaged mental state, be tried today. Based on our decisions, the Registry has taken measures that have led to very successful surgery of my client, the accused Erdemovic, and the psychiatrists and psychologists have managed to calm his disturbed mental state. Everything was done to make the accused Erdemovic competent to stand trial today, as stated in the conclusion of the international expert team. Your Honours, the limits of this trial were set by the indictment of the Prosecutor, but also by the things that Erdemovic pleaded guilty to. As the indictment has not been amended in the meantime, I will now make some observations. I have read the indictment several times with due care as the document itself and the trial warranted. Every time I had to ask myself why it was written in this form in respect to the accused Erdemovic, particularly because the first part is not based on any evidence presented in this trial. Here I refer to paragraphs of the indictment 1 to 8 and paragraph 14 of the indictment. As I searched for the answer to that question and read the Nuremberg trial documents, I found substantial similarities between the indictment, this indictment, and the indictment issued by the Board of Prosecutors of the International Military Tribunal in Nuremberg. However, in reality, these were two very different affairs. Allow me a digression: The International Military Tribunal, pursuant to Article 6 of its Statute, was competent to, and I quote "try and punish major war criminals of the countries of the European Axis, to try and punish persons who either as individuals or as members of organisations committed any of the crimes sanctioned here acting in the interests of the Axis countries" and so on. So not only individuals, 22 of them, but also criminal organisations of the Nazi Germany were on trial in Nuremberg. A whole era, a regime, was on trial and the Board of Prosecutors was bound to include in the indictment the collective responsibility as the results of the era and the activities of that regime. This Trial Chamber, however, of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia tries an individual, my client, the accused Erdemovic. The fact that these parts of the indictment against him refer to a general military and political situation in Bosnia and in Srebrenica, in particular, does not have any factual foundation and any legal foundation in the Statute or the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal, nor in any evidence presented, nor does it have anything to do with the accused Erdemovic. The Statute of this Tribunal, Article 6 - there seems to be a coincidence here with the Statute of the International Military Tribunal - stipulates that the Tribunal is competent to try only individuals and not any collective entities. I am referring to governments, parties, military leaderships, police forces and so on. That is one point. Another point, the way this was described in the indictment, the accused Erdemovic did not contribute at all to the military and political situation described in the indictment. He was not a military Commander. He was not a person with political authority. He was not even close to the persons who bear the most responsibility for this cruel war which could give rise to any assessments of the general military and political situation in relation to his deeds. On the contrary, he was (as were so many others from all warring factions) a victim of the cruel war and its horrors. That is why I appeal to you, to your honourable Judges, to reject that part of the indictment against Erdemovic in all respects and especially in respect of his contribution and culpability for the situation, and also in respect of the fact that this part of the indictment cannot affect the degree of responsibility of Erdemovic for the acts he had pleaded guilty to before this Trial Chamber. That is why the judgment of the Trial Chamber must only refer to the evidence, facts and the degree of the responsibility to which the accused Erdemovic pleaded guilty. In other words, the contents of paragraphs 9 to 12 and partly in paragraph 15, qualified in paragraph 16.1, of the indictment as crimes against humanity. As regards that part of the indictment, specific charges against my client Erdemovic, in my closing argument I will first assess the evidence presented here and the establishment of the relevant facts. I will deal with the facts from the point of view of criminal law. So let me proceed. As regards the act itself, the only direct piece of evidence presented before the Trial Chamber is the statement of the accused Erdemovic given under oath. In this statement he actually incriminated himself and defended himself at the same time. The self- incrimination in his defence concerned mostly the following facts. On 16th July 1995 a group of eight members of the 10th Sabotage Unit, Sabotage Corps of the Serbian Army, received the order to go to Zvornik and report to the military police command. The accused Erdemovic was in this group and he had no idea of what kind of assignment it would be. Upon their arrival in Zvornik and a short stay there, the group went together with an officer from the military police command to the farm near the village of Pilica. On the farm, for the first time, the group Commander informed the members that Muslims would be bussed to the farm and that it was their task to shoot those Muslims, and an order was issued to that effect. The accused Erdemovic immediately opposed the order, but the Commander's response was typically military and brooked no opposition: "If you don't want to do it, you can line up next to them". In such a surprising situation, the accused Erdemovic was not able to resist the order. According to his statement, he feared greatly for his life and the lives of his family. His whole body shook and his mind went blank. Against his own will he obeyed the order of his Commander and fired in the direction of the innocent Muslim civilians who had been brought and lined up there. Because of the state he was in, Erdemovic does not know how many Muslims were shot that day, least of all how many of them he shot himself. This figure cannot be checked. He knows that it lasted from 10.00 in the morning until 4.00 in the afternoon. During the shooting, the accused Erdemovic tried to free a Muslim but failed. He and the other members of the group all refused to carry out the task of shooting Muslims in the cultural hall in Pilica. This was followed by days of struggle to find the bare necessities of life and the fight for his life and long sleepless nights with no end in sight. The facts, as I have stated, were established only on the basis of Erdemovic's testimony. So if the Trial Chamber decides to give credence to his plea of guilty, then they should also trust these facts, because his statement is a logical one and proved by the life itself. The Prosecution has also accepted these facts and they mentioned them in their closing argument. We have just heard that. As for the subjective elements which are important in judging this case, and they are important and objective for me, but the importance of subjective elements in the Nuremberg trials was, let me remind you, illustrated by a psychologist of the International Tribunal, Mr. Gilbert, in his book "The Great Criminals" and the English writer and lawyer Airey Neave in his book "Nuremberg". So, as regards the psychological attitude of the accused Erdemovic towards the act, his current mental state and his character in general, in addition to his own testimony, the Trial Chamber heard witnesses X and Y, two reports of an international team of experts were obtained on the psychological and psychiatric condition of the accused Erdemovic. There is also the report on his general health. So based on this evidence, I deem that the following legally relevant facts have been established beyond reasonable doubt. The accused Erdemovic on 25th of this month will be 25 years old - five years that he has spent in war. He is a Croat and a Catholic but never paying too much attention to that. His childhood and boyhood days were happy in the place where he was born, in the vicinity of Tuzla. He was a good student at school. He liked school, especially because of the friends he had there. He socialised with everybody, regardless of their religion or nationality. Those questions were simply never asked. He was brought up as a Yugoslav and that is how he felt himself to be. He loved his country, former Yugoslavia. We have heard that from him today. He thought that it was the most beautiful country in the world with most freedom. He enjoyed sports very much, especially football. He was a fan of "Red Star" in Belgrade and he is still a supporter of "Red Star" in Belgrade. In 1991, he was proud when he came to that same town, Belgrade, to do his military service. But when the war broke out in Croatia in July 1991, as a soldier of the Yugoslav Army, he went to Slavonia with his Unit but did not take part in any of the fighting around Vukovar. After completing his military service in March '92, he returned to his home where he was first mobilized into the Muslim army and then into the HVO who arrested him because he had tried to help Serbs. Because he had no choice, in November 1993 he fled to the Serb-held territory and then he roamed in Serbia for a while. Later he joined a Unit of the army of Republika Srpska because he had no other possibility. As a member of a Unit of the army of Republika Srpska, he never took part in any actual direct combats or any similar assignments. However, as the war drew to its end in a situation which I have described, sudden and unforeseen, on an order of his Commander he took part (as he himself had said) in the execution of Muslims. He stated to the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and to the investigator of the Tribunal, Mr. Ruez, to psychiatrists and to the psychologists, he stated the same thing that he stated before this Trial Chamber. It is contained in all records that were composed in relation to those interviews. After that this calvary of war was followed by his personal calvary and that of his family. He was unable to support his family and himself. He took his wife and son to their parents and he remained in Bijeljina and took to drinking. He felt unsafe because he was called "Ustasha" because of his Croatian origin. Then on 22nd July 1995 in a cafe in Bijeljina a fellow fighter shot him and two of his friends. His wounds were serious and life threatening. He underwent surgery three times. While he was treated at the Military Medical Academy, he was visited by only one of his brothers-in-arms. He was bitterly disappointed at losing them too. Although he did not have any objections to the way he was treated by the Yugoslav authorities, he wanted to be tried by this honourable Tribunal. However, he still suffered a serious form of post-traumatic stress syndrome as stated by the experts in their report. He was very hurt by the fact that his close relatives have had problems because of him. The accused Erdemovic has lost everything. He has lost his home, not only because of his destiny but also because of the destiny of other people, innocent people, and he suffers because of that a lot as he bears everything with himself and one can say that it is with certain uneasiness but it is very hard for him. I would like to stress that on the basis of the evidence heard, certain very important facts have been established, importance which will enable to establish criminal responsibility of the accused Erdemovic. The Judges and investigators of this Tribunal were not aware of the events in Pilica not until the accused Erdemovic started speaking about that, not until he incriminated himself. This fact is accepted by my learned colleague from the Prosecution. The testimony of witness X confirmed the statement of Erdemovic that when he was in a position as a soldier of the army of Republika Srpska to decide on the fate of a member of an opposing army, he set him free and he saved his life. Likewise, when he was in the HVO, he tried to help Serbs, but he was caught and imprisoned. From the very first statement to the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia until the statement given under the oath before this Trial Chamber, he admitted to the participation and the commission of the act and thereby brought himself to justice, showing his moral attitude towards the crime. I will tell you something. Personally, I admire this behaviour of my client and why. Immediately before he gave a statement to the investigators of this Tribunal, I advised him to change his statement, the statement that he gave to the authorities, the plea that he gave to the authorities of Yugoslavia. Throughout the proceedings he expressed his attitude about the fate of the innocent people. Throughout the proceedings he has clearly co-operated with the Prosecutor without any plea bargaining, as the Prosecution has confirmed. Your Honours, as far as I am concerned, these are the relevant facts in judging this case. However, when I had to draw some legal conclusions I stumbled upon the issue which legislation to apply, especially when it comes to the basic concepts of criminal offence, the possible full defence is necessary self-defence, extreme necessity, caution, duress, criminal responsibility, degree of capacity, mental capacity, premeditation and so on. The reason is that because these concepts are not regulated in the Statute and the Rules of this Tribunal. I found the following reasons why this was not done, and I think that from the stand point of legality it had to be done, first, because these concepts are generally accepted in most laws and are regulated in more or less the same way or, secondly, that international commissions established after Nuremberg did not accomplish one of their tasks and that is to codify international criminal law. That is why in drawing my legal conclusions I referred myself to judgments, theory and practice of legal jurisdictions, including my own country which is what the provisions of the Statute and the Tribunal encourage in a way. So, given the situation with the statutory provisions, my view is that the evidence heard and the statement of facts which I mentioned before point to the following two legal attitudes that can be taken in respect of this criminal case. Firstly, and it is a hypothesis, it was necessary to answer the question whether the crime alleged in the indictment has been proved beyond reasonable, that is, whether the confession of the accused Erdemovic is sufficient proof that the alleged crime was actually committed. Judgments of the court's legal theory and practice often indicate that in order to reach a judgment in a legal matter, the confession of an accused is not enough. It should be corroborated in other evidence. This is why I insisted on that particular point yesterday, because Erdemovic's plea of guilty and the explanation given by his counsel must be confirmed so that a Court can reach an objective and legally acceptable judgment beyond any doubt. My intention was not to challenge Erdemovic's plea on his behalf. However, according to the principle in dubio pro reo, certain questions arose yesterday. Your questions, your Honours, also had that tone. That was the impression that I had yesterday. Because I believe, your Honours, that if there is any shade of doubt in that answer to that question, then the decision of the Court should go in favour of the accused Erdemovic, because regardless of his plea of guilty, if his statement is not corroborated, the alleged crime cannot be proved and the criminal responsibility cannot be established. However, today we have heard many details. My second legal opinion has for its basis the determination of this Chamber that the evidence heard confirms the commission of the alleged crime and corroborates his statement. In that case all the above mentioned facts and circumstances enable me to include the following. First, that the accused Erdemovic committed the alleged crime out of extreme necessity, that is, in face of the present danger for his life.
