This concept is accepted in the Criminal Codes of all European jurisdictions. Allow me to elaborate on this. The Austrian Criminal Code of 1975 in its Article 10 provides for the extreme necessity which excludes guilt. The Belgium Criminal Code of 1967 stipulates in its Article 71 that "there are no crimes or offences when the perpetrator was under duress which he could not resist". The Greek Criminal Code speaks of the existence of the extreme necessity as grounds for the exclusion of illegality and guilt. The Hungarian Criminal Code from 1961 in its article 26 stipulates that the perpetrator who has committed the criminal offence out of extreme necessity shall not be held responsible. The criminal code of Finland, article 10, provides for the possibility of discharging for the act committed out of extreme necessity. The Dutch Criminal Code, article 40, stipulates that an act shall not be considered as punishable if committed under duress or coercion. The French Criminal Code, article 64, stipulates that there shall be no offence if the accused at the time of the commission of the crime was under duress which he could not resist. The German Criminal Code from '75, articles 34 and 35, provide for the extreme necessity which excludes criminal responsibility. The Swiss Criminal Code from '37, article 34, stipulates that the perpetrator who has committed offence out of extreme necessity shall not be punished especially if by doing so he was saving his own life. The same is provided for in the Swedish criminal code from 1965, Chapter 24, Article 4. The criminal code of Yugoslavia from 1977 in its Article 10 provides for the extreme necessity which excludes the very act but provides for the possibility of acquittal. Historically speaking, it is a long tradition of a certain concept, but the very essence of the concept of extreme necessity is the same as the one described in the criminal code of France from 1870. The concept of extreme necessity is accepted in the legal theory and judicial practice both as a range of subjective theories which lead to the discharge of the perpetrator, or a range of objective theories which all boil down to the non-existence of the public danger and the illegality of the crime or else as a theory of individualization, according to which all cases of extreme necessity cannot have the same type of defence which would justify an acquittal. The stated position that the accused Erdemovic committed the alleged crime in a state of extreme necessity can be confirmed with the following facts. I have to repeat them. The accused Erdemovic was a member of a unit which was ordered to carried out an execution of Muslim civilians. This is stated in the indictment. So, together with seven other members of his unit, on the relevant day he found himself in situation which he could not foresee or anticipate. When the Commander issued out the order he had no idea of what kind of assignment it was. He tried to resist the order, but he did not succeed. Moreover, it was indicated to him that he too would be shot. Fearful for his own life and the life of his family, the accused Erdemovic, against his own will and in a disturbed state of mind, took part in the execution. As a soldier, a Croat fighting on the Serbian side and always a potential traitor, he had to obey the order and not his consciousness. He could not resist the order in any possible way. One can say that he was instinctively protecting his own life and the life of his family which were his highest values contained in the declaration on human rights. It is not moral to expect that he should have sacrificed his own life and then quite certainly the life of his family. Finally, even if he had done that in relation -

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are speaking a bit too fast, Mr. Babic. If you could slow down a little bit for the sake of the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BABIC
utterances.text: I believe it is not moral to expect that he should have sacrificed his own life first and then, quite certainly, the life of his family too. Finally, even if he had done that, that would not have helped the innocent victims and he would have been shot with them. Your Honours, I remember an historic event from the Second World War in Yugoslavia. A German dared, so to speak, to refuse orders, to disobey orders, and he refused to shoot innocent civilians. He simply took the side of the civilians. He was shot and the civilians were shot too. At his initial appearance before this Tribunal he himself said: "Honourable Judges, I had to do that. If I had refused to do it I would have been killed together with these people. When I tried to refuse the order they told me: 'If you feel sorry for them, go and stand in the same line with them.'" This is what he repeated yesterday and today several times. Therefore, the accused Erdemovic in a specific situation was exposed to an unavoidable, psychological type of duress which was beyond his capacities and which he could not resist. Therefore, your Honours, I request that he be acquitted. This is provided for in all the above stated documents, either as an obligation or as a possibility as far as extreme necessity is concerned. In relation to this request, I wish to point out two other very important issues. The issue of the accused Erdemovic's mental responsibility at the time of the commission of the crime and the issue of his premeditation at the time the crime was committed. Although these issues were not specifically examined by medical experts, that is neuro-psychiatrists and psychologists, I believe the experts who were hired by the Court presented sufficient elements on the basis of which it would be possible to draw reliable, factual and legal and psychiatric conclusions on the state of the mental responsibility and the premeditation of the accused Erdemovic at the time the crime was committed, both on his awareness of the seriousness of the crime and on his will to commit it too. The elements I am referring to are the following: emotional immaturity, that is what it says decidedly in the expert report; the feeling of helplessness at the time and after the crime; panic and fear at the time the crime was committed; an obvious long-lasting post-traumatic stress disorder. These elements are supported by other elements which have been established beyond reasonable doubt in the proceedings so far, the fact that even after refusing to carry out the order, after the unsuccessful refusal to obey it because he was fearful for his life, the accused Erdemovic was no longer conscious of his acts, he literally did not have nor could he have had any freedom of will. He did not want to commit the act of his own will. It was the will of the command. Then, your Honours, the following legal conclusions have to be drawn. The accused Erdemovic at the time of the commission of the crime lacked mental responsibility because he suffered a temporary mental disorder or, at best, his mental responsibility was significantly diminished also. In the case of the accused Erdemovic there was no premeditation at the time of the commission of the act because he did not want to commit it. Based on these legal premises and on this basis, I seek that the accused Erdemovic be acquitted. Your Honours, my professional experience makes me cautious. I see this caution in possible failure to accept my views as presented here on the existence of extreme necessity and lack of mental responsibility and premeditation in the accused Erdemovic, and the failure to agree to my request that he be acquitted. In that case, I deem the facts that I use to establish extreme necessity and lack of mental responsibility and premeditation, as well as the facts I presented regarding the character of the accused Erdemovic should be taken into consideration as special mitigating circumstances when the sentence is passed. May I repeat this once again. The accused Erdemovic barely managed to stay alive and he lost everything else. His next of kin are not left in peace. He lost his comrades. He lost his country. He came to realise that in this war all civilisational values were rejected in this war, that all traditional ideas of morality, justice and law have been replaced by somebody's needs and interests. He believes that the individual his liberties, rights and requests would not survive as such. Is there a worse way of using and abusing a man? Is there a graver punishment? The basis for passing a sentence is envisaged in Article 24 of the Statute and Article 101 of the Rules of Procedure. In this connection, I believe it is very important that this Court takes into account hitherto experience in the world and in the former Yugoslavia and to find in this context the right position and role of the accused Erdemovic and to determine the degree of his responsibility. Allow me to quote some of this experience. In the Nuremberg trials 22 people were tried, the main war criminals of fascist Germany. Twelve were sentenced to death, three to life in prison, four to imprisonment from 10 to 20 years respectively and three were acquitted. It is well-known that this was the political and military leadership of Germany, whose crimes had killed millions of people and brought awful terrors to the world. Further on, the verdict of the American Tribunal from February 19th 1948 against high Nazi military commanders headed by Field Marshal Liszt, out of 12 accused for war crimes and crimes against humanity two were convicted to life imprisonment and six to time in prison from seven to 20 years. At the trials of main war criminals in Hungary similar sentences were passed. As a source for that I use the book "Genocide and Punishment" whose author Dr. Lajco Klajn is a Professor at the University of Novi Sad. The main criminals who were tried in the former Yugoslavia after the Second World War also received the highest sentences too. As a source for that I use the book "Through the Secret Archives of UDBE" of the well-known Yugoslav writer Nikola Milovanovic. The accused Erdemovic is not a Field Marshal nor any kind of military Commander. He is not a Minister. He is not the head of a criminal organisation, nor the main culprit. In the structure of the army of Republic Srpske he was a plain soldier. That is why there is not a place for him on that ladder in terms of his role, in terms of what he did, in terms of his degree of responsibility or in terms of possible imprisonment. If by some circumstance this Tribunal were to try all of those who committed crimes in the former Yugoslavia, then it is also quite certain that the accused Erdemovic would be in the group of the least responsible, or perhaps he even would not be in that group at all. Regrettably, your Honours, in this closing statement I cannot present the punishment determined by the courts of the former Yugoslavia to others, that is to say, not to the main perpetrators of war crimes in the Second World War, simply because these verdicts have not been compiled in one place. The country fell apart and archives fell apart. One thing is certain, that most of this punishment was time in prison and that most of the convicted persons did not stay in prison until the end. In determining punishment before this Court the Statute and the Rules of Procedure also refer to legal solutions in Yugoslavia. In this connection I presented to a brief to the Tribunal. I just wish to repeat. For the criminal offence of war crimes against a civilian population, which is an act stipulated in Article 142 of the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia, a sentence of imprisonment from five to 15 years was envisaged or imprisonment of 20 years. Also in the brief I said that there was a legal possibility of mitigating such a sentence. This mitigation can go up to one year of imprisonment. All of the above-mentioned mitigating circumstances, the elements provided by the Statute and the Rules of Procedure, as well as legal provisions in the penal code of Yugoslavia, give me a basis for suggesting to this honourable Court to considerably mitigate the sentence passed on the accused Erdemovic. I am profoundly convinced that in this particular case that is the only sentence that can be fair, not only for him but also for the victims. Even more so because there are, in my opinion, no aggravating circumstances in the case of the accused Erdemovic. In this connection, we cannot take into account as an aggravating circumstance the death of several persons as the Prosecutor said, because this element is included in the very being of the crime and this is determined by the level of responsibility of its perpetrators. May I summarise by saying that I ask this honourable Court to acquit the person, to pass a sentence mitigated by at least one year. In connection with a possible jail sentence, it is very important where it will be served. In the Statute and the Rules of Procedure there are certain provisions referring thereto. I do not want to declare myself directly on this question now. I believe that such a decision should be passed without the presence of the public. But my request and the wish of my defendant is that if he serves time that this be done in a western European country where the system and conditions of imprisonment are at a high level. Your Honours, at the end of this closing statement I wish to say before you and the distinguished representatives of the Prosecution, before the entire public, in my own name and on behalf of the defendant, that these criminal proceedings were conducted in keeping with the Statute and the Rules of Procedure, but that is not to say that these two documents should not be further improved upon. On the contrary, I think they should. But I also wish to say that these proceedings have been conducted fairly and honestly. They were conducted and participated in by people of high professional and moral qualities, which shows how lofty this profession is. Through this and through all other trials every one of us can only draw a humane lesson and a message which will, like a memento mori, be transferred to all people worldwide, regardless of where they live and what they do. Everyone who receives this message and who draws on this experience will be able to distinguish what truly happened on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, what reality is, what the truth and what propaganda and lies are. Let the Court of history pass judgment on us and also the Court of legal science and practice which is inevitable. Let them show that we have done everything well and in the interests of justice. In your decision, our decision, may the main message be that these terrible experiences do not be repeated and that mankind does not fall into the abyss of war horrors once again. I am confident, your Honours, Judges of this highest criminal institution of the international community, that when passing your decision in this case through your knowledge of the facts and your understanding of reality you will show humaneness towards the accused Erdemovic through a decision which will give him hope for a life of love, not of hatred. That is what the accused Erdemovic looks forward to and sincerely hopes for. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Babic. As we had said, the Trial Chamber will now listen to a final statement by the accused, if he cares to do so. The accused will not be under oath. Mr. Erdemovic, is there anything you would like to add, a brief statement which as, I said, will not be under oath? If you care to stand and make such a statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If it is more convenient for you to remain seated, please remain seated. Otherwise you may have some problems with the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, it is OK. First of all, honourable Judges, I wish to say that I feel sorry for all the victims, not only for the ones who were killed then at that farm, I feel sorry for all the victims in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina regardless of their nationality. I have lost many very good friends of all nationalities only because of that war, and I am convinced that all of them, all of my friends, were not in favour of a war. I am convinced of that. But simply they had no other choice. This war came and there was no way out. The same happened to me. Because of my case, because of everything that happened, I of my own will, without being either arrested and interrogated or put under pressure, admitted even before I was arrested in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, I admitted to what I did to this journalist and I told her at that time that I wanted to go to the International Tribunal, that I wanted to help the International Tribunal understand what happened to ordinary people like myself in Yugoslavia. As Mr. Babic has said, in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia I admitted to what I did before the authorities, judicial authorities, and the authorities of the Ministry of the Interior, like I did here. Mr. Babic when he first arrived here, he told me, "Drazen, can you change your mind, your decision? I do not know what can happen. I do not know what will happen." I told him because of those victims, because of my consciousness, because of my life, because of my child and my wife, I cannot change what I said to this journalist and what I said in Novi Sad, because of the peace of my mind, my soul, my honesty, because of the victims and war and because of everything. Although I knew that my family, my parents, my brother, my sister, would have problems because of that, I did not want to change it. Because of everything that happened I feel terribly sorry, but I could not do anything. When I could do something, I did it. Thank you. I have nothing else to say.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Our deliberations are now complete. The Tribunal will render its decision within approximately two weeks. A specific date which will be transmitted through the press and information office. The Court stands adjourned. (4.30 p.m.) (The Court adjourned)
